As IoT applications move to the edge, they face unique challenges such as supporting real-time processing for multiple events occurring at once, dealing with limited resources, and ensuring low-latency communication. Developing edge applications requires a suitable framework that addresses these difficulties by incorporating event-driven programming and efficient evaluation techniques. To facilitate building such applications, we propose a new language model that incorporates event-driven processing and draws from existing database query languages. This model compiles to a range of edge runtime environments, including those based on SQL, MongoDB, and Apache Flink, eliminating the need for explicit deployment instructions. This approach results in more compact, efficient, and scalable code, and is paired with a tool that automates the evaluation process, enabling developers to focus on applying updates and handling ETL (extraction, transformation, loading) processes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a case study on an IoT scenario from the telecommunications industry. Furthermore, our edge runtime manager supports multiple compiler backends and enables dynamic migration of applications across different edge environments. This management layer, combined with a user interface for database schema visualization, facilitates easier database schema integration and provides more versatile options for edge application development. This, in turn, produces more effective and optimized applications for edge environments. This research is now part of the Helium Oranges project at the University of Innsbruck. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. These findings have significant implications for the current LHC program and will converge with future upgrades of the ATLAS detector in the course of the LHC's ongoing development. A benchmark for the ATLAS experiment's future in the context of the HL-LHC is also outlined with a focus on rare processes. This study is an expansion of earlier reports presented at LEPC and now reflects the most up-to-date information available from the ATLAS experiment. Its contents will be relevant through the year 2024 in its current form. The development of advanced driving technologies requires vast datasets of realistic traffic scenes to facilitate training. To date, commonly used datasets are limited due to the extensive time and resources necessary to collect and annotate them manually. Our proposed system, SceneGen, tackles this challenge by combining a generative model with a user-friendly interface that allows multiple users to contribute simultaneously. SceneGen utilizes a conditional generative neural network to generate realistic traffic scenes from a variety of starting images, and through repeated iterations, refines its results for better accuracy. By leveraging both user-provided reference scenes and datasets, SceneGen improves the diversity of generated scenes. The team presented SceneGen at the "Traffic Scene Generation" workshop at the 2021 Conference on Computer Vision, and the system's capabilities were evaluated through both qualitative and quantitative assessments, with results showing significant improvements in generated scenes compared to a baseline model. The source code for SceneGen is publicly available on GitHub. One potential application of SceneGen involves using generated scenes to create custom training datasets for autonomous vehicles. A combined ergodic property for sequences of integers is defined as a theoretical concept that builds upon combined recurrence and combined distribution properties. These properties are properties of sequences that maintain their original form under specific transformations, such as addition or multiplication by certain integers. A combined ergodic property enables these sequences to converge in average to their mean value after a certain number of terms, regardless of their initial position within the sequence. This concept is utilized to demonstrate combined ergodicity for sequences of nonnegative integers arranged in a specific order, based on their ratio of terms. Specifically, if the ratio of two sequences, resulting in a new sequence of integers, has a combined distribution property, and a third sequence, derived from the ratio of the first two sequences through multiplication by certain integers, possesses a combined recurrence property, then the first two sequences will exhibit a combined ergodic property. Furthermore, this relationship can be applied to prove the combined ergodicity of sequences of positive real numbers, following a specific order based on their ratio of terms. Additionally, the paper explores combined ergodicity within sequences of integers or positive real numbers within a specific range, as well as its connection to ergodicity within periodic or quasi-periodic sequences. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, presents significant difficulties for deep learning-based object detection systems. The problem is compounded by limited annotated data sets that cover this range. Notably absent in existing datasets are annotations that indicate the slight distortions in bounding boxes when objects are far from the camera. The commonly used annotation tools for bounding boxes assume a coordinate system where the (4th, 5th, 6th) coordinates represent the box's 3D dimensions, but this model is inaccurate for far-field objects. As a result, the evaluation metric for far-field detection, mean average precision (mAP), is inaccurate due to systematic errors. To address this issue, a new evaluation metric called far average precision (farAP) is proposed, along with Far3Det, the first dataset annotated for far-field detection with corrected bounding boxes. Far3Det is based on the MMD17 dataset and consists of 3,561 annotated far-field objects from 198 point cloud scans. When tested on the dataset, deep learning models performed better on near-field objects, but far-field detection results were less impressive due to difficulties in distinguishing between nearby objects, especially those in the far field. Notably, farAP scores varied more greatly between models than the standard mean average precision metric, indicating that farAP is more sensitive to model performance. Despite the challenges, model performance improved on retraining with the Far3Det dataset, with one model achieving a farAP score of 11.3% on the dataset, a 5.5% increase from the previous best result. The study also evaluated the impact of increasing the size of the dataset through addition of near-field annotations, finding that farAP scores improved significantly, with a score of 25.7% achieved on the expanded dataset, indicating that far-field detection models still require large amounts of data to perform well. Far3Det and the proposed farAP metric provide a more challenging and realistic evaluation of the capability of deep learning models for far-field detection, making them a valuable resource for advancing the field. The code for Far3Det and the proposed evaluation metric farAP is available at https://github.com/christianmeyer/far3det, and the dataset itself is available at https://christianmeyer.github.io/far3det/. We introduce a novel approach to creating chemistry sampling layers for quantum machines that can efficiently produce high-quality approximations of ground states for molecular compounds. By leveraging a quantum neural network named the chemistry ansatz and incorporating a gradient-based optimization process, we effectively transform classical neural network techniques such as batch normalization and batch regularization into quantum applications. The resulting chemistry sampling layer can prune unnecessary single-particle orbitals based on their relevance to the ground state, thus providing a meaningful orbital selection procedure. The chemistry batch regularization method is introduced to address the issue of orbital growth during the optimization process by limiting the increase in overlap between orbitals. Our experiments demonstrate impressive accuracy improvements for various molecular compounds when using our proposed chemistry sampling layers in combination with a quantum neural network, achieving average absolute errors of 0.89 kcal/mol for conformation analysis, 1.13 kcal/mol for isomer differentiation, and 0.17 eV for bond distance prediction. Furthermore, a significant reduction in orbital growth is observed, from 0.48 for traditional neural network optimization to 0.16 with the chemistry sampling layer. The introduction of chemistry sampling layers enables the simulation of larger molecular compounds by addressing the scalability issues associated with the neural quantum model, such as orbital growth and single-particle basis size. With these layers, we successfully simulated compounds with 20-40 atoms by accurately predicting energies with an average absolute error of 1.36 kcal/mol. The implementation of these layers paves the way for the further development of quantum machine learning models capable of processing complex chemical processes and predicting the properties and behavior of various compounds. The source code for the proposed chemistry sampling layers can be found at https://github.com/hhaosheng/qml-chemistry. The numerical experiments were performed using a total of 1024 qubits on the IBMQ backend with a max gate size of 23. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. We anticipate our benchmark to contribute significantly to the development of robust scene flow estimation algorithms. Code and benchmark data are available at https://github.com/mandenghui/sf-benchmark for reproduction and extension. We also explore the integration of our proposed framework with additional training data through partial supervision, showcasing its potential in accelerating self-supervised flow estimation using LiDAR data. Motion trajectory production using LiDAR and stereo cameras is compared to showcase the advantages of our method over supervised flow estimation. Ultimately, we achieve results on the VMR-7 dataset that outperform the current state-of-the-art by a margin of 45.95, equivalent to 0.162 in metric units. This significant improvement emanates from precise replication of the target flow trajectories as evidenced by a flow error reduction of 0.175. In-depth evaluations using various protocols and metrics confirm the excellence of our method, highlighting its robust performance through multiple repetitions. Moreover, we find that simple model variations, like changing the batch size, can result in distinct performance trends and even guide the model towards inferior outcomes, emphasizing the importance of thorough evaluation procedures in computer vision research. In light of these findings, we stress the need for transparent performance assessment, incorporating multiple repetition flows for accurate evaluation, and we propose the use of a suitable metric such as the scale-independent mean square error for flow evaluation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets. Compared to its static counterpart, this proposed network exhibits a key advantage of achieving the same level of accuracy with significantly reduced computational operations, thus also leading to a real-world demonstration of energy savings in actual deployment. Furthermore, overcoming the challenge of synchronizing spikes across different neurons allows the network to achieve even higher levels of efficiency, resulting in a significant improvement of up to $4.5\times$ in overall performance. We believe this idea has the potential to create a new path for the development of more sophisticated neuromorphic networks that combine high performance with low power consumption and minimal computational resources. We hope this version provides a clearer and more comprehensive exploration of this concept. In addition to addressing several key limitations of the original proposal, we have also introduced a new technique for expanding the network's capacity to process more complex data sets with smaller numbers of neurons, showcasing the proposed network's capability to achieve accurate results on larger datasets such as the ImageNet. Nonetheless, applying this approach to such large datasets also requires further investigation into optimization techniques that can fully utilize the network's full potential. We have made the source code for this project publicly available on GitHub, and it has also been successfully replicated on the NeuPy Spiking Neural Networks Library using a range of different hardware platforms. We have also successfully demonstrated the proposed network's performance on a wide range of unstructured classification datasets, including those with multiple classification outcomes, using both simulated and actual hardware configurations. We have explored various optimization techniques that can further improve the performance of this network, especially when processing larger data sets. We have successfully expanded this project to include multiple classifiers using both simultaneous and sequential training methods, and has also been successfully demonstrated on a range of structured data sets, such as text and graph classification. We have investigated several techniques that can further improve the performance of this network, especially when processing larger data sets

By leveraging these structures, we are able to efficiently colour the edges of these graphs. Additionally, our findings correlate the presence of Hamiltonian cycles with the parity of a specific number, which is derived from the graph's orientation. Ultimately, our results provide a general ideal number for this class of graphs, although the Hamiltonian Number (the minimum number of Hamiltonian cycles required) may vary. Therefore, we decide to focus on the edge colouring aspect under the name Ideal Number. By doing so, we are able to prove that this number is equal to half of the graph's chromatic number, further demonstrating the relationship between edge colouring and our ideal number through an equation. This conclusion is achieved by showing that certain edge colourings meet the ideal number condition due to the presence of Hamiltonian cycles, which allows us to utilize a proof similar to that of a related theorem. On the other hand, we are also able to find examples of graphs for which the ideal number is not equal to half of the chromatic number of their complements. By doing so, we raise a question related to the removal of edges from a graph, which could be viewed as a variation of a question related to the addition of edges to a graph. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies within containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops continuously audits a program's system calls and builds upon a rules-based language to create and manage a set of temporal rules. These rules enable Timeloops to predict future legitimate system calls, allowing it to create a reduced filter for the program's secure operation. We demonstrated the effectiveness of Timeloops by applying it to the evaluation of temporary system data persistence and verified its performance on various benchmark tests. Furthermore, an open-source implementation of Timeloops is made available for others to use and review. We found that, on average, the learning and prediction capabilities of Timeloops result in a 30% more compact system call filter, compared to an optimal static solution, with only a 10% increase in processing time. Additionally, the review of our code by other researchers yielded no security vulnerabilities. We discovered that, with the help of Timeloops, the system call learning module for the Apache HTTP Server could be optimized from 22MB to 13MB in size. This optimized version has since been incorporated into the official Apache HTTP Server codebase. We are currently exploring methods to extend the scope of system call filters learned by Timeloops to other aspects of system security. As a result, we propose the development of an additional module for Timeloops that would determine whether a given first-order temporal logic policy can be implemented as a system call filter. This potential new feature would provide programs with an additional means of ensuring their own security. We already have a working prototype of this feature, which we refer to as Timeloops-Soft. Investigating global $B-L$ symmetry within the Standard Model is necessary due to the anomaly cancellation requirements which necessitate three right-handed neutrinos that enable the natural generation of small Standard Model neutrino masses through the seesaw mechanism. Within an augmented Standard Model, we introduce a $B-L$ symmetry, gauged but unbroken, and explore global $B-L$ symmetry breaking to describe pseudo-Goldstone Dark Matter. The model includes a fourth generation of partially interacting right-handed neutrinos. The Dark Matter candidates emerge as long-lived pseudoscalars, scalarons, or vectorons resulting from the $B-L$ symmetry breaking at an extremely high temperature. The model's parameters are constrained by guidelines on neutrino mass generation and the consistency of the electroweak symmetry breaking. Speech generation demands not only linguistic rules but also implicit social norms and contextual understanding. Despite significant progress in speech generation technology, current systems often produce stilted or nonsensical outputs, particularly when confronted with changes in setting, tone, or character traits. To address these limitations, we introduce MaskedSpeech, a context-aware speech production model that utilizes masking strategies to incorporate external contextual cues. By transforming contextual information into masked speech-related tasks, MaskedSpeech learns to generate more coherent and natural language. Experimental results show that MaskedSpeech achieves substantial improvements in coherence, grammatical correctness, and overall naturalness. Furthermore, we demonstrate MaskedSpeech's ability to handle complex contextual inputs, such as narrative scenarios, by successfully integrating external character traits, settings, and tone into the speech generated. A distinctive feature of neurogenesis in the developing vertebrate brain is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelium as interkinetic nuclear migration unfolds. Despite widespread occurrence, the underlying mechanics of this phenomenon remain largely unexplored. Utilizing high-sensitivity two-photon imaging and precise time-stamping in live zebrafish retinas, our study reveals that nuclear movements conform to a continuous diffusion model, with varying levels of constraint depending on the retina's axis. The results of our analysis indicate that nuclear migration speeds are consistently high across the epithelium, with an average speed of approximately 3.1 micrometers per minute. The data further reveals a remarkable lack of directional preference in nuclear movement within the plane of the epithelium, as well as an almost imperceptible radial gradient in nuclear migration speeds. The observed retention of high migration speeds deep within the layers of the neuroepithelium challenge existing theories that reduce nuclear migration speeds in the interior layers due to space constraints. Furthermore, our research reveals that the time it takes for a nucleus to complete a full migration cycle is directly proportional to the time spent in each layer, demonstrating a novel aspect of interkinetic nuclear migration. The findings of our study offer a revised understanding of the mechanics underlying interkinetic nuclear migration, with implications for our current knowledge of cell cycle dynamics, retinal cell production, and the allocation of progenitor cells within the vertebrate brain. In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. To enhance coded adaptive binary maximal probability permutation (CABMPP) codes, which are commonly used for compressed sensing, we propose a decoding approach that outperforms existing methods. By exploiting the specific properties of these codes, our method surpasses general compressed sensing decoders, such as the maximum likelihood estimator, for certain code parameters. As a result, our proposed decoder yields better estimated images when compared to state-of-the-art methods in color image demosaicing and compressed video recovery. Moreover, our approach facilitates efficient computation using a streaming algorithm, reducing the required operations by a factor of eight to 25, depending on the code parameters. Ultimately, our proposed decoder excels in compressed video recovery, outperforming even the optimal maximum likelihood estimator. Consequently, our code variants perform better than random codes for certain parameters. Our method's efficiency, combined with the high quality images produced, make it an ideal choice for compressed video recovery and demosaicing. Moreover, our work provides a framework for further optimization of coded modulation methods used in compressed sensing. In particular, our results suggest that future research should focus on enhancing the performance of code parameters with low variability, as these are currently underutilized due to the dominant impact of compressed sensing constraints. As a result, there is considerable room for performance improvement beyond the established limits. Furthermore, our work raises the question of whether compressed sensing with high-performance codes is feasible in color image demosaicing and compressed video recovery. As a solution, we introduce a new class of simple and efficient codes, called low-variance coded adaptive binary degenerate code (LVCABC) codes, which are particularly well-suited for these applications. LVCABC codes have the advantage of providing high-performance estimates at significantly lower computational costs, making them highly desirable for real-world applications. Furthermore, our work also provides a new approach for the reconstruction of compressed videos using LVCABC codes, leading to a data rate reduction of at least 5 dB compared to standard compressed sensing methods. As a result, our work on LVCABC codes offers a new path for further optimization of compressed sensing codes, especially for codes with low variability, and we anticipate that future research along this direction will yield significant performance improvements. Building on Aberdeen Tunnel's unique location, this project aims to develop a device for investigating spallation neutrons. Aberdeen Tunnel is situated near a natural abundance neutron source in Aberdeen, where fast neutrons generated by cosmic rays interacting with atmospheric molecules, specifically oxygen and nitrogen, produce unique outcomes in the tunnel's underground laboratory due to its deep depth of approximately 22 meters. Nevertheless, the production of spallation neutrons, which are produced when cosmic rays collide with atmospheric molecules, is not as well understood. To tackle this, we plan to utilize the Aberdeen Tunnel Laboratory's underground environment and natural abundance neutron source by utilizing a 4π solid-angle neutron detector system consisting of three types of sensors: a $^3$He neutron detector, a plastic scintillator detector and a liquid scintillator detector. By combining data from these sensors, we can accurately identify fast neutrons generated by cosmic rays and analyze the production of spallation neutrons. This device will significantly contribute to our understanding of these neutrons, which play a crucial role in the development of nuclear reactions and the creation of cosmic rays' secondary particles. This, in turn, will help in the optimization of neutron sources for experimental use, such as neutron scattering and production of radioactive isotopes. This research project has the potential to deepen our understanding of neutron interactions with nuclear reactions and atmospheric molecules, which will further facilitate the development of new neutron sources for scientific experiments. This novel device will also provide valuable insights that can be applied to the detection of spallation neutrons in underground laboratories across the world. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is openly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey, suitable for any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation. The TKS dataset can be found at https://teksurvey.info/, along with the sifting algorithm used for our sample selection. The effectiveness of this approach is illustrated through the analysis of several key properties of the TKS targets, which reveal intriguing patterns on the planets' sizes, orbital periods, and host stars' temperatures. The findings of this study can be applied to any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation, and the target selection strategy described is openly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey, suitable for any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be measured through light curves as the YORP effect induces periodic variations. We calculated the YORP effect and rotation velocity of three asteroids, (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos, utilizing their light curves and orbital data with the aim of identifying a possible increase in rotation velocity due to the YORP effect. We determined the YORP value and rotation velocity of these asteroids for the first time and found that the YORP effect is positive in all three cases, indicating that their rotation velocities are increasing over time. Furthermore, our results show that (10115) 1992 SK and (1620) Geographos are close to a chaotic state as a result of the YORP effect, while (1685) Toro is on the edge of a chaotic regime. Our study also provides estimated parameters for the moment of inertia and surface texture of these asteroids and highlights the importance of continuous light curve observations in determining the YORP effect and rotation velocity of asteroids. Additionally, we discuss how multiple observations of light curves can reveal the YORP effect and rotation velocity of these small bodies more accurately. Finally, we suggest that the YORP effect can lead to asteroids entering a state of chaotic rotation, resulting in irregular light curves, and potentially increasing the likelihood of an asteroid becoming a binary or phossilith. Overall, this study demonstrates the significance of light curve observations in determining the YORP effect and rotation velocity of asteroids and highlights the need for continued monitoring of these small bodies. We demonstrate that any countable collection of surface homeomorphisms, preserving a curve, is relatively compact within the space of surface homeomorphisms that contain a fixed curve homeomorphism 'u'. This statistical property is established using techniques from dynamical systems and topology. Moreover, our findings prove a key requirement for homeomorphisms 'f' and 'g' to have related dynamics: the presence of a homeomorphism 'h' that, combined with iterations of 'f' and 'g', results in a topological expansion equivalent to that of a quotient map derived from 'h'. This outcome is a fundamental contribution to understanding the relationship between surface homeomorphisms and their associated dynamics. Finally, we show that groups generated by homeomorphisms 'f' and 'g' have a compact subset within the space of homeomorphisms that preserve a curve, providing a key application of our main theorem. This achieves a key goal of establishing the relatively compact property for groups of homeomorphisms 'f' and 'g' on surfaces without a global topological equivalent to a quader. This property is a crucial component in proving the continuity of shift homeomorphisms associated with surface homeomorphisms 'f'. Consequently, we are able to demonstrate the continuity of shift homeomorphisms for a broader class of surface homeomorphisms than previously established. This is a key component in previously unresolved problems concerning the continuity of boundary translation operators. Finally, we show that groups generated by homeomorphisms 'f' and 'g' are locally compact within the space of homeomorphisms that preserve a curve, providing a key application of our main theorem and a key component in previously unresolved problems concerning the continuity of shift homeomorphisms and boundary translation operators. This achieves a key goal in establishing the continuity of shift homeomorphisms and boundary translation operators for a broader class of surface homeomorphisms than previously established. 

On the other hand, we provide an example to show that there exists an uncountable collection of hyperbolic surface homeomorphisms whose closure within the space of surface homeomorphisms that preserve a curve is not relatively compact. Moreover, we demonstrate that any countable collection of curve-preserving surface homeomorphisms whose boundary translation operators have a continuous shift homeomorphism-related property is relatively compact within the space of surface homeomorphisms that contain a fixed curve homeomorphism 'u'. Precise stellar characteristics are vital for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, particularly when studying M-dwarfs. Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can be used to estimate stellar parameters such as temperature, luminosity, and mass. However, these relations often rely on broad-band optical observations that can be misleading due to the scars and spots on low-mass stars, particularly below 0.5 solar masses. As a result, researchers need to utilize UV spectroscopic observations to determine the stellar parameters for M-dwarfs, as they allow for measurements of photospheric metal absorption that are crucial for accurately calculating the stellar parameters. This initial study of the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample examines the process of selecting field M-dwarfs with the appropriate observational data, assesses the accuracy of stellar parameters obtained from empirical relations, and explores potential systematic errors. This study has identified a regression analysis that provides the most accurate estimates of stellar parameters using UV and optical spectra. It has also established a protocol for evaluating data quality and identified sources of scatter in the data, which includes overall activity levels, activity patterns, and Koniggay-Seyfert diagrams. This protocol will be utilized to select the most reliable data and provide a foundation for evaluating and selecting the most accurate stellar parameters for the M-dwarfs in the UV Spectroscopic Sample. This study delves deeper into the theory by demonstrating that a stack of two similar metasurfaces can achieve significant ripples through a nonlinear interaction with normally incident light. However, this arrangement presents difficulties when attempting to redirect or increase the ripples through external means. In contrast, a separated architecture of two distinct metasurfaces has been found to linearly respond to varying incidence angles, enabling control over the ripples through external influences such as electric fields. Although the main goal of testing database consistency has been understood since 1979, when the first results in this area were published, research has slowed down over the years. To regain momentum, researchers need to analyze current outcomes from testing various database queries. With the development of sophisticated testing methods for simple queries, the focus has shifted to more complex queries involving self-joins. This research provides an in-depth examination of how existing testing methods perform on these complex queries, especially those with at most three distinct tables and no cycles between them. Specifically, it evaluates current testing methods' ability to accurately determine whether two instances of these complex queries are equivalent or not. This evaluation considers multiple aspects, including the presence or absence of certain database structures, symmetry in the queries, and the number of possible connections between different tables. To better understand the practical applications of these queries, the research involves generating random, yet meaningful, queries that are relevant to real-world databases. It also assesses the efficiency of both deterministic and randomized testing methods when dealing with these complex queries, including whether they can determine equivalence in a finite amount of time. Additionally, it explores the challenges associated with developing more comprehensive outcomes from testing these queries and suggests potential answers to this question. The mean absolute deviation from the median has gained significance in recent times due to its robustness to outliers, which makes it a desirable statistic in data analysis.  Despite the presence of outliers, conventional bias estimation techniques can be applied to the mean absolute deviation because its bias is manageable.  Specifically, a normal approximation and a bootstrap bias correction have been proposed as effective methods for bias reduction.  Interestingly, the standard bootstrap estimate can also be utilized to correct the bias, and intriguingly, this simple approach proves to be at least as efficient as the normal and bootstrap methods.  Furthermore, the standard bootstrap estimate exhibits a notable advantage in terms of computation, requiring substantially less computational effort compared to the other methods.  Additionally, an interesting phenomenon is observed where the standard bootstrap estimate tends to over-correct the bias, resulting in an estimate that is at times even less biased than the original mean absolute deviation.  This paper provides a comprehensive bias analysis, including a formal bias presentation, and confirms the bias's asymptotic and large sample equivalency.  A simulation study and a real-world example are also included to illustrate the bias's behavior and its effectiveness in comparison to other methods. As the largest power of a prime that divides $n$, $\omega(n)$ captures key properties of the integer distribution, making it significantly harder to compute than prime factorization. By showcasing calculations for specific values and intervals, this paper demonstrates its relationship with the Dickman $\rho$ function, which is notoriously challenging to compute directly. We establish an alternative, efficient method to determine $\omega(n)$ through the use of sieve inequalities, revealing that it is comprised of two distinct components with different growth rates. While $n$ contains a prime power of size approximately $\sqrt{n}$ with a probability of around $n^{-\rho(2\ln n)}$, this relationship serves as a sensitive probe of the prime number distribution, as it is linked to the assertion of the Prime Number Theorem. Furthermore, our work provides a more sophisticated understanding of $\omega(n)$ for larger values of $n$, while the associated problem of determining $\omega(n)$ given computational access to $n$ remains an open question of computational number theory. Additionally, we propose a working definition for the term "fragile" in mathematics, capturing its essence through the distribution of $\omega(n)$, particularly in the context of large values of $n$. Finally, we explore potential applications of both $\omega(n)$ and its associated distribution in mathematics, statistics, and computer science. While it is known that $n$ has a prime power of size approximately $\sqrt{n}$ with a probability of around $n^{-\rho(2\ln n)}$, our work provides a broader perspective on this phenomenon, revealing that it is not isolated and that values of $n$ with extremely large or extremely small ratios of integral components are far more common than one would be led to believe based on computationally determined values alone. In fact, even after removing prime powers, $n$ still has a power of approximately $\sqrt{n}$ with a probability of around $n^{-\rho(2\ln n)}$, indicating that this phenomenon is not merely a result of the distribution of prime numbers. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-based method known as Multiple-Choice Knowledge Promoting (MCKP), which employs vast amounts of textual information to facilitate self-improvement.
This method incorporates a selection process that involves consistently presenting models with conflicting answers, thus helping them identify the correct response and fine-tuning their performance using high-confidence results.
As part of the FLAN evaluation suite, we design five tasks to explore models' ability to generalize across similar tasks, differing only in modified prompts, and find that both T0 and FLAN exhibit better cross-task generalization after MCKP when compared to alternative methods like self-supervised learning and few-shot shooting. Moreover, our analysis reveals that these models can successfully generalize to some extent, but ultimately struggle with adapting to significantly varied tasks with limited access to contextual information. Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a differentially private deep learning model without utilizing real datasets is therefore crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to simultaneously address the hyperparameter tuning and differential privacy constraints. The framework is applied to a customfully designed private deep learning framework, and an algorithm with a privacy cost significantly lower than the current state-of-the-art is introduced. The proposed algorithm achieves a balance between high performance on the test dataset and compliance with the differential privacy standard, essentially solving a complex multi-objective optimization problem. The framework and algorithm are rigorously evaluated using real-world datasets for our deep learning model, and the results indicate a substantial improvement over the current state-of-the-art in terms of hyperparameter tuning. Furthermore, the framework is adaptable to various hyperparameter tuning algorithms, making it a versatile solution. The code for this paper is openly accessible on the GitHub platform. This research aims to simulate the thermomechanical process for microstructure development resulting from strain-induced crystallization during injection molding. Strain-induced crystallization occurs when amorphous polymer chains transform into a crystalline state in response to mechanical stress. This process involves complex interactions between temperature, strain, and time, often referred to as coupled conditions. To accurately capture its effects, our model incorporates a nonlinear relationship between crystallinity and strain, a heat generation term, and a phase change equation. By applying this model to an experimental elastomeric material, we successfully simulated the onset of crystallization and measured the resulting crystallinity. Our simulation also indicated a non-uniform crystallinity distribution in injection-molded parts, confirming previous observations. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of cooling rate and strain on crystallinity. Our findings indicate that increasing the cooling rate or initial strain can lead to a higher crystallinity level. This model has the potential to predict the microstructure development of elastomeric materials in various processing conditions, enabling the design of materials with optimized properties. Our simulation model can also be applied to other polymers exhibiting strain-induced crystallization. To verify our model's accuracy, we compared our simulations with scanning electron microscope images showing the material's surface morphology. By integrating this model with numerical optimization techniques, we can identify the optimal processing conditions to produce elastomeric materials with desired microstructure properties. Our model can be applied to injection molding but may require modifications to accommodate other processing methods. Our research also highlighted the importance of considering the initial anisotropic microstructure of polymers in their material properties. By taking this into account, we can simulate the material's behavior during processing and resulting microstructure development. This knowledge can be utilized to model the behavior of polymers in various processing conditions and is essential for understanding the complex phenomena involved. Sequential neural network models are renowned for their versatility in processing
linearly sortordered sequences, including those inherent to human language.
Context-free grammars, on the other hand, provide a versatile framework for
describing language structures and serve as a robust foundation for computational
models of human language.
Recent studies have demonstrated the capability of neural network-based models
to replicate logical deductions from context-free grammars, but only in a
linearly sorted order determined by the model's sequential structure.
Our investigation aims to exceed this limitation by having the model learn
from raw text to infer semantic properties over a particular language (Basque)
using a simple neural network model (LSTM). We establish a new computational
framework for understanding the conjunction/contradiction implications of any
sentence in context-free grammars and assess the performance of this system. We
find that only a small subset of the most fundamental rules are easily learned
by the LSTM, but it has difficulty in discovering more complex ones, even when
faced with an extensive corpus of text. We discover that this limitation is
not due to the nature of the neural network but rather the weak logic it is
based on, as demonstrated by our proof that any neural network based on this
logic will have the same difficulties. We further find that this system is
not unique to LSTMs and that other sequential neural network models exhibit the
same behavior. Finally, we show that this system is quite different from two
other systems: one based on a linear model of semantics and another on a highly
advanced neural network model. Ultimately, we conclude that this system is
more in line with the linear model of semantics but there is a key difference:
while the baseline is capable of learning all the rules from the corpus, our
system can only learn a subset of them, indicating a greater need for further
understanding of the relationship between the learning capabilities of this
system and the structure of human language. We also propose a potentially
meaningful distinction between two types of logic: one that is inherent to the
rules governing the language and another that emerges from the actual use of
the language, and we anticipate that exploring this difference will yield a
deeper insight into both the nature of human language and the capabilities of
these systems. Additionally, we raise the question of whether the failure of
these systems to discover more complex rules from the corpus is an indication
of a broader limitation of neural network models in capturing the implications of
concord in human language,

The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggfortify in ggplot2) graphical tools. This package is an R language variation of the Python implementation for Local Fisher Analysis (LFA) developed by Remi Fondaoui. The lfda R package is an open-source implementation available on CRAN. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike traditional optimization-based methods that rely on exact robot dynamics models, imitation learning can compensate for modeling inaccuracies and facilitate the learning of complex motions from sampled sub-critical trajectories. Despite its advantages, imitation learning has limitations, primarily involving the generation of feasible and safe trajectories to meet nonlinear constraints and avoid obstacles. To address these challenges, we introduce Extended Kernelized Motion Planning (EKMP) as a generalization of imitation learning framework, capable of processing linear and nonlinear constraints, feasible space mapping, and obstacle avoidance. EKMP builds upon the success of kernel-based methods by combining conditional kernel mean embedding with a feasibility mask, allowing for the extraction of feasible data points and construction of a feasible space map. This feasibility mask also enables gradient descent optimization to produce constrained trajectories along with a formulation for handling obstacles through potential field-based feedforward trajectories. The evaluation of EKMP is conducted across multiple scenarios, including linear and nonlinear constraint cases, comparing its performance to state-of-the-art imitation learning approaches. A graph G is considered a serial extension of a monarchy M if every connected component of G corresponds to a path in M. The maximum weight of subsets of edges in a serial extension of M is denoted as w(M)* and is equal to the maximum weight of subsets of edges in M. We aim to find the maximum weight of subsets of edges in a serial monarchy M with edge weights subject to certain constraints. This weight is optimal for a graph G if it satisfies the condition: every connected component of G corresponds to a path in M. We prove that this optimal weight can be achieved if and only if G is a serial extension of a subgraph of M that contains all maximal cycles in G. We also develop an algorithm based on this equivalence that efficiently determines whether a given serial monarchy has a specified weight and finds the most constrained subgraph of M. Additionally, this algorithm establishes a polynomial size representation of the optimal weight of a graph G, significantly improving a previous exponential-size representation. The discovery of binary asteroids is crucial to understanding their physical and orbital characteristics, which can be compromised without simultaneous observations of both components. By analyzing the Pan-STARRS1 survey images, our machine learning model identified 28 potential binary asteroids, including the specific binary asteroid (6) Hebe, and submitted these findings to the Minor Planet Center for verification. However, further examination revealed inaccuracies in some predictions, which can be attributed to astrophysical obstacles such as false positives from asteroids with irregular shapes and the inability to accurately assess the likelihood of such events occurring. Furthermore, our study revealed that the most promising candidates for binary asteroids are those with orbits in the asteroid belt's inner region and those that have distinguishing features in their light curves. Nevertheless, our study laid the groundwork for future research in this field. By utilizing the Pan-STARRS1 sky mapper and the upcoming Zwerty telescope, we will be able to recover and verify the binary asteroids predicted in this study and pinpoint additional binary asteroids lurking in the vast dataset of available images. This approach will enable us to recover and verify the binary asteroids in (4) Vesta, (10) Hygiea, and (16) Psyche, three of the largest asteroids in the belt, and provide accurate measurements of their binary asteroid counterparts. This in turn will provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of the asteroid belt and make possible the verification of results from numerical simulations of the binary asteroid population. This research is crucial for unlocking the full potential of the Pan-STARRS1 dataset and setting the stage for the Zwerty telescope's groundbreaking observations of the solar system. We encourage researchers to utilize this model for detecting additional potential binary asteroids and to submit these findings to the Minor Planet Center for verification. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' actions based on past behavior, their past actions in relation to the game's overall objectives, and the characteristics of different identities, which in turn helps it select the most effective ways to steer the players towards desired outcomes through conversation. Human assessors evaluate our system's ability to manage multiple player characters simultaneously by guiding them in a series of Dungeons and Dragons scenarios. Our results show that a learned Dungeon Master can successfully guide players toward a common goal over the course of several Dungeons and Dragons scenarios, surpassing a baseline model that doesn't incorporate the same level of understanding of game characters and objectives. This improvement supports the feasibility of using a Dungeon Master representation for assessing a system's ability to manage other identities within a narrative setting. Our research also explores the implications of introducing new game characters to the players, incorporating their intentions and the influence of their past actions on the game world, which in turn informs our understanding of multi-id interactions in Dungeons and Dragons. These considerations contribute to the development of a more comprehensive handbook that can guide the creation of artificial intelligence dungeon masters for various types of role-playing games. Our research in this domain has been made publicly available through an AI Dungeon Master Challenge on GitHub, which includes all the methods and evaluation tools used in this study. These tools can be used to create AI dungeon masters for other role-playing games, which in turn can be tested against a range of scenarios defined by the protocols and tools we've developed in this research. Our work has also been presented at an academic conference and discussed with the broader Dungeons and Dragons community to ensure that the methods and metrics used in this research are usable and relevant to both the scientific community and the game's players and moderators. Which in turn has led to the publication of this research in an academic conference. Despite significant research, understanding lexical semantic variation across languages remains a major challenge in computational linguistics. Existing approaches to capturing word meanings and performing cross-language comparisons have primarily focused on individual words, neglecting the inherent semantic relationships within words' meanings. This overlooks the underlying lexical semantics of each language, which are essential for comprehending word meanings. Our approach addresses this limitation by incorporating a combination of contextual word representations and distributed semantic models to characterize word meanings and their semantic fields. We apply this method to analyze the lexical semantics of two languages, English and Spanish, using a dataset rich in contextual information. Our results show that our approach reveals meaningful semantic structures in both languages and distinguishes between their vocabularies with high accuracy, outperforming existing models. Furthermore, our method's variability-based framework identifies significant lexical semantic variations between the two languages, which we validate through human annotations. Our approach and data are now available for further exploration of lexical semantic diversity across languages. To overcome this limitation, we propose the development of phrasal hypotheticals as a distilled form of counterfactual text that expresses plausible scenario structures. Moreover, DISCO, an explicit counterfactual reasoning model developed in conjunction with this framework, significantly outperforms alternative methods in evaluating the coherence and likelihood of generated counterfactuals. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique pinhole-equivalent structure. However, this structure transitions to a remote epitaxial configuration when vacuum is applied during growth, or to a van der Waals epitaxial structure if a native hydrogen layer on graphene is removed. The transition between these modes can be understood through the surface energy of GdPtSb that becomes unstable on graphene, leading to an empty lattice. This research offers guidance on selecting Heusler compounds that could successfully form remote epitaxial structures with graphene. Moreover, it highlights the possibility of controlling film equilibrium through vacuum or surface passivation, which could be applied broadly to various thin film systems. The findings of this research may also lead to the discovery of new remote epitaxial materials and structures when combining complicated band structures with unique electronic properties, such as those found in Heusler compounds, with the versatile graphene substrate. The research involves experimental observations, supported by simulation and discussion of the underlying physics. It demonstrates the capability of graphene as a remote epitaxy substrate, capable of supporting the equilibrium of complicated Heusler films that are highly lattice-mismatched. The research lays the groundwork for exploring remote epitaxy on graphene with various compounds, that could provide unique properties, such as the half-Heusler compound LaFeCO, a suitable hydrogen storage material. The research also shows that most previous and current images of Heusler films grown on graphene, are actually representing structures of pinhole or van der Waals epitaxy, rather than remote epitaxy. It offers a new method for distinguishing between the different epitaxial structures, by analyzing the energy and surface of the Heusler compound, that becomes empty on graphene, leading to a unique pinhole-equivalent structure. The research provides concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process, that overcomes the barrier of high lattice mismatch, that could be applied to other systems, that could provide unique properties, such as the half-Heusler compound LaFeCO, a suitable hydrogen storage material. The GNS construction is a well-known method for creating a representation of an algebra within a Hilbert space, derived from a positive linear functional. Dittmann and Landahl generalized this process, allowing for a family of positive operators to be used in place of the original linear functional. We have further expanded upon their work by establishing a connection that enables us to begin with a state and the corresponding algebra of observables, leading to a representation of the algebra within a Hilbert space. This process can be seen as a realization of a functor associated with the algebra, within a category of Hilbert spaces equipped with unitary intertwiners. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful training for wearable healthcare applications relies heavily on utilizing a large quantity of cross-device data, which poses a significant challenge due to the restrictions of data sharing allowed by personal data protection policies. A possible solution to overcoming these limitations is through the employment of federated learning, a technique that enables multiple device owners to collaborate in training a shared model without exchanging data. However, the usual approach of utilizing similar cross-device datasets directly poses another issue, as it fails to account for the differences in data distributions across devices and the presence of noisy data, which significantly reduces the effectiveness of this method in wearable healthcare. In response to these limitations, this study introduces FedHealth, a transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare that incorporates federated learning. FedHealth incorporates several innovative mechanisms including explicit regularization, data normalization, and a diverse sampling strategy for optimizing cross-device training. Through comprehensive experiments, FedHealth demonstrates its capacity to handle complex wearable healthcare datasets efficiently and accurately, achieving impressive results on three diverse datasets and outperforming alternative methods by substantial margins in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, FedHealth's performance is complemented by a user-friendly interface that provides transparent and secure code, alongside a project repository available on GitHub. With its cutting-edge technology and exceptional performance, FedHealth is well-suited to handle various wearable healthcare tasks. Additionally, this study explores the practical applications of FedHealth through real-world deployments with multiple partnering companies, highlighting the framework's potential for collaborative cross-device healthcare projects. Overall, FedHealth represents a groundbreaking breakthrough in wearable healthcare, enriching the field with robust methods for handling complex, cross-device datasets and enabling the development of more effective healthcare applications through seamless collaboration between devices and companies. This leads to a more comprehensive understanding of users' healthcare situations and enhances the performance of healthcare models. As such, FedHealth is an ideal example of pioneering work on federated learning in wearable healthcare, and its codebase serves as a leading open-source framework for shared healthcare datasets. With its groundbreaking technology, FedHealth paves the way for the creation of more reliable and versatile healthcare models, capable of processing a wide variety of healthcare data across devices. This, in turn, facilitates the development of more effective and versatile healthcare applications, as well as a deeper insight into users' healthcare situations. By examining the underlying mathematics, we also obtain a result that could be useful in its own right, regarding the existence of a common ground between two different ways of measuring the distance between states. Temporal sequence learning typically involves extensive labeling efforts, which can be costly and prohibitive in many settings. In this study, we explore the application of guided learning to single-point measurements in life sciences, such as cell counting and protein expression analysis, where samples are typically labeled, along with their corresponding temporal sequence images. Our primary objective is to develop a guided model that can accurately predict labels for individual measurement points within temporal sequences, with minimal reliance on explicit annotations. We successfully demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through the prediction of spatial features, such as counting cells and identifying protein expressions, as well as the classification of sequence segments, including determining whether a region of tissue is cancerous or benign, all without labeling individual measurement points. Our technique also enables the enhancement of measurement accuracy for certain samples, integrating information from adjacent measurement points. We have made our code publicly available on GitHub. In addition, we have conducted further experiments to investigate the implications of guiding single-point measurements with neighboring points, particularly in the context of combining models for averaging predictions. This approach helped us identify a method for producing low-variance predictions, achieved by selecting sequences with diverse trend patterns. We have incorporated this strategy into our code as well. We have also explored the application of our technique to guided multi-point measurement problems, such as determining the structure and function of genes, by developing a novel neural network architecture that efficiently exploits labeled sample points, resulting in significant performance gains. We have extended our original code to incorporate these modifications and changes. We have further investigated the guided learning of temporal sequence data through the application of neural network architectures, such as multi-layer perceptrons, recurrent neural networks, and transformer models, as well as the integration of prior knowledge, such as genetic data, into the modeling of life sciences measurement points, further enhancing the efficacy of our approach. We have incorporated these modifications and changes into our code as well. We have also conducted a comprehensive study on the guided learning of temporal sequence data through the development of a simulation framework, by exploring various neural network architectures, the impact of prior knowledge, and the effect of diverse sequence patterns, and making our simulation framework available openly on GitHub. We have integrated all these changes into our code as well. We have examined the application of guided learning to single-point measurements in life sciences, including cell counting, protein expression analysis, determining whether a region of tissue is cancerous or benign, and the study of gene structure and function, through the use of neural network architectures, such as multi-layer perceptrons, recurrent neural networks, and transformer models

Additionally, it is demonstrated that this problem can be solved via an algorithm, and further explores related problems of both optimal sequence reconstruction and hamming distance calculation. Further, it is shown that this algorithm applies to other metric distances that are closely related, such as the Lee distance, by transforming these distances into equivalent hamming distances. This research expands on previous studies by addressing sequences that are not ordered. Research on musical instrument recognition has long been an important area of study, with numerous applications including entertainment, education, and medical fields. Although advances have been made, there are still challenges to be overcome, particularly with certain types of instruments and in complex acoustic environments. One such technique with promise is multi-task learning, which has been successfully applied to image recognition tasks by combining low-level features with high-level semantics. However, when it comes to audio signals, the process is more complicated due to the underlying hierarchical structures of music sounds. To address this, we propose a novel method called hierarchical multi-task learning, which leverages the natural organizational patterns of music sounds to improve the recognition of musical instruments. This method involves breaking down the classification into a series of nested challenges and developing a customized optimization approach to enhance the learning process. To support our claims, a comprehensive experimental evaluation is conducted, showing significant improvements over existing methods and the unique benefits of each component of our proposed approach. Interestingly, it is also observed that the best performance is achieved with a relatively simple implementation, far from the complicated deep learning models commonly used today. This work contributes a thorough analysis of the underlying music sound structures and their implications on instrument recognition, along with an open-source code available online. To facilitate future research, we also introduce a new dataset called MIR-54, consisting of 54 classes of musical instruments, along with 5500 training and 1100 testing audio files. This dataset has the unique feature of containing a diverse range of instruments and provides a more realistic representation of actual musical performances. To further expand the scope of research in this area, we also introduce a new challenge called the instrument recognition relay, which involves identifying the next instrument based on the previous detection in a relay race-style classification process. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of the art in musical instrument recognition, along with analysis of the best existing methods and the proposed approach. To conclude the paper, an overview of potential future research directions is also presented. This work has been presented in two conferences, ICML 2021 and ICASSP 2022, and has been recognized as one of the top submissions in the later conference. To facilitate future research, this paper also introduces a new leaderboard for musical instrument recognition, along with the evaluation metrics used. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of the art in musical instrument recognition, along with analysis of the best existing methods and the proposed approach. To conclude the paper, an overview of potential future research directions is also presented.

Ph.D. candidates in computer science spend significant time reading research papers to stay informed, but they often struggle to discern important, novel information due to the overwhelming volume of content. A major obstacle is the absence of a dataset that enables machine learning models to link relevant information in papers to previously unknown concepts. To address this limitation, we've created a dataset called QPA, which comprises more than 10,000 human-annotated triples consisting of a research paper, a target concept, and a corresponding question designed to discover new information related to that concept. These triples are divided into two categories: 14 high-level topics, such as computer vision, natural language processing, and machine learning, and 5 less specific areas of study. We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. Our study reveals that in the presence of the linear potential, the Majorana fermion exhibits average properties similar to those of the free Fermi gas, despite individual instances displaying significant fluctuations. These fluctuations are particularly pronounced when the particle is trapped between its resurrection and creation points. This effect is found to decrease as the linear potential increases, ultimately leading to a situation where the average entropy values approach a constant thermodynamic equilibrium. This phenomenon may be observable in not-too-small systems, provided the necessary conditions are met. Additionally, we demonstrate that Majorana fermions are more susceptible to entropy fluctuations when compared to their Dirac counterparts. This difference arises from the distinct ways these particles interact with their surroundings, with the Majorana fermion displaying increased sensitivity to its environment due to the larger influence of the external linear potential on its energy spectrum. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of fully overlapping DNA strands can represent both a parent and a child object, with the difference between them being the specific sequence of nucleotides. This design allows for easy updates by swapping out the nucleotide sequence of a given object, whereas changing the primer pair requires a more involved process involving the hybridization of two separate strands. Furthermore, we describe an algorithm for creating a hierarchy by recursively organizing objects based on their DNA content and propose two methods for updating data, including one that utilizes a pair of complementary strands and another that makes use of a third helper strand. The performance of our storage system was evaluated through a series of experiments utilizing PCR for both testing and proof-of-concept demonstrations of the proposed algorithms. The results show significant improvements in storage efficiency, with a typical object occupying ~13-14% of the available DNA length, in comparison to the 20-50% typically required by other systems. The revision times, measured through the PCR cycle time, show that our approach allows for rapid data updates, taking around 1 hour for 200 objects, in contrast to the more time-consuming re-synthesis methods employed by other systems. Furthermore, the proposed PCR-based sorting technique offers a means of organizing large amounts of stored data, with an estimated time of ~1 day needed to sort ~36,000 objects. The DNA storage system, along with its supporting techniques, marks an important step in the development and implementation of large-scale DNA data storage platforms. Our aim is to present a framework that combines the strength of profound learning models with the causality expertise, allowing them to learn causes and effects more effectively by incorporating a representation of graph causality within their neural network framework.  This integrated approach involves generating a graph representation of the data's underlying causality and incorporating it into the neural network's framework to guide its predictions.  This approach has shown superior performance in comparison to standard neural networks in multiple settings, particularly in scenarios where only limited quantities of data are available.  Our method has been found to result in models that not only perform well but also provide valuable insights in the form of a causal graph.  We have tested this approach on real-world images and time series data using state-of-the-art profound learning models and have made several key observations: our method delivers enhanced performance, produces models with strong generalization capabilities, and has the ability to filter out noisy data by only incorporating information that is consistent with the data's underlying causality.  Notably, our method has demonstrated significant improvement in performance over standard neural networks, with performance increasing by a multiple of at least five in certain scenarios.  Our approach has several key advantages, including the ability to integrate prior knowledge into the data's causality graph and the ability to handle multiple variables simultaneously.  Our technique has several potential applications, including the creation of realistic virtual environments and forecast models, particularly in domains where variables can take any value.  Our method can also be used to provide physical constraints to models that learn variables' functional relationships, such as models that learn the physical properties of materials, the behavior of animals, or the movement of objects. A comprehensive understanding of temperature distribution in catalytic fixed bed reactors is crucial for ensuring safe operation, preventing hot spots, and optimizing catalyst efficiency through thermal management. However, determining temperature distribution requires knowledge of inlet flow rates, reaction rates, and heat transfer coefficients, which can be difficult to obtain to a satisfactory level of accuracy. As an alternative, the concept of an observable temperature arrangement can be explored, characterized by a single statistical measure that incorporates thermal gradient information. A study employed rapid magnetic resonance imaging to investigate the temperature arrangement in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor under flowing gas, revealing that it is significantly affected by flow rates, as evidenced by the formation of temperature oscillations in both laminar and turbulent flow regimes. Increasing the inlet temperature or withdrawing heat from the bed has a calming effect, while shifting the temperature arrangement to a more complex state. A regulatory mechanism governing the transition between oscillatory and gradient states was observed, demonstrating that high Reynolds numbers can suppress oscillatory arrangements, thereby potentially optimizing reactor performance through flow rate control. The findings of this study may be interpreted through a nonlinear interaction between heat transfer, convection, and diffusion, providing a framework for further theoretical analysis. The proposed framework also facilitates the use of Arrangements Networks, a set of abstract variables, to monitor and understand the behavior of complex thermal systems. The results of this study are also relevant to the broader context of complex systems, highlighting the importance of examining variables in an arrangement-based framework, as it can reveal hidden interconnections and regulatory mechanisms that are indicative of a system's high level of autonomy and robustness. The study employed the imaging technique described in the paper by Li et al. The researchers used a catalytic fixed bed reactor consisting of a cylindrical bed filled with 500 micrometer sand particles and a nitrogen flow that was also used in the previous study. The temperature distribution within the bed was visualized through rapid magnetic resonance imaging while varying the flow rate, inlet temperature, and heat transfer coefficient. The study discovered a more complex variable called the temperature arrangement that characterizes the distribution of heat within the bed. The temperature arrangement switched to an oscillatory state as the flow rate increased, and this transition was prevented by fixing the flow rate at a high value. The arrangement was also shifted to a more complex state by withdrawing heat from the bed. The study demonstrated that high Reynolds numbers can suppress oscillatory arrangements, suggesting that flow rate control could optimize the performance of these types of reactors.
