Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. Using two-photon polymerization, we fabricated and experimentally validated microscopic acoustic metamaterials, successfully redirecting incident waves and verifying that a 0.29 wavelength-thick microacoustic metagrating can efficiently allocate 90% of transmitted energy into the -1st diffraction order. This work is the first successful implementation of two-photon polymerization in fabricating complex acoustic metagratings in the ultrasound frequency range, which we believe will serve as a prototype for even more intricate structures in this range. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an open-world cross-entropy loss framework. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that this proposal results in a dynamically adjusted confidence threshold. This paper analyzes two techniques for repairing fences: self-downgrade and self-invalidation. It demonstrates that using these techniques in combination can significantly reduce the number of repairs required by implementing the Porterfield-Schlichting algorithm. Specifically, it shows that if processes follow a program order, only one repair is needed for each update, depending on whether a specific location is read-only or read-write. It also presents two different implementations of this algorithm, along with performance and scalability results derived from simulation and actual execution. These results indicate that this combined approach yields a notable improvement in performance and a substantial reduction in memory usage, which could provide the basis for further optimization strategies. It is also shown that the self-downgrade policy can be achieved through the use of atomic memory locations, though this would imply that no repairs are needed for updates to such locations. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this context, Freiman's 3k-4 theorem can be seen as a special case where the condition is met when a specific element of B is chosen. This selected element of B then exhibits considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. It's further proven that this strengthened version of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem has significant implications on the growth of subsets of integers, implying that the exponent of this growth could be as low as three-quarters. This is achieved by a new approach to the problem and this new approach is applicable even when the number of possible summands available from subset B is much higher, specifically up to n*k instead of 4*k. The classical Wreath product for groups is a versatile construction that maintains many desirable properties, such as being abelian or nilpotent, depending on the characteristics of its components. It also forms a universal object that is compatible with functors, making it closely related to the notion of a universal construction. The wreath product for simplicial sets, however, does not directly retain these beneficial characteristics due to the inherent nature of simplicial sets being directed. Instead, we introduce the universal simplicial collection, which serves as a comprehensive analogue to the classical wreath product, while also demonstrating that it constitutes a simplicial group. This result is established through a pairwise action between the universal simplicial collection and Set*, leveraging the principles of category theory to derive this conclusion, as well as through a direct construction that is rooted in the properties of simplicial sets. Both approaches are presented in the paper. Furthermore, we explore the connection between the universal simplicial collection and simplicialemergence, which includes the universal simplicial set. This paper builds upon the earlier work of A. Boucheron and G. Rovelli in "The classical wreath product is a group in the category of simplicial sets". The class of groups that can be represented as wreath products of simplicial sets encompasses a wide range of group structures, including all countable groups comprised of a torsion-free abelian group with a finite base and a nilpotent group with a solvable order. Notably, it also includes several uncountable groups, such as a countable group that is both torsion-free and of the first kind, as well as a diverse array of non-abelian groups, including all simple groups, with the exception of the 2-generator group in the variety defined by the identity $x^2=y^2$. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the universal simplicial collection, simplicialemergence, and simplicial sets that are homeomorphic to subsets of a Euclidean space, establishing that the universal simplicial collection corresponds to the simplicialemergence of such sets and that it forms a simplicial group that is both abelian and nilpotent. The degree of nilpotency of the universal simplicial collection is determined to be two for abelian groups and three for non-abelian groups. This paper delves into the source of high false positives in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD), a task that involves identifying two objects and the relationship between them within an image. After conducting an in-depth analysis, we discovered that the main issue lies with the excessive creation of additional pairs of objects that are not present in the ground truth data. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced when incorporating additional features through a matrix factorization technique known as Graph Attention Network (GAN). In order to address this problem, we propose a novel detection framework called Dual-Phase VRD (DPVRD). This framework is designed to minimize the creation of unnecessary relationships by introducing a relationship prediction phase that reduces the object pair space before making a final detection. Our approach achieves this reduction through the use of a binary mask to eliminate superfluous relationships and employs a score normalization method called Non-Negative Norm (NNN). By systematically evaluating our approach on three challenging datasets (Visual Genome, Visual Relationship Detection Dataset, and OpenImages), we demonstrate significant improvements in accuracy and a substantial reduction in false positives when comparing DPVRD to the current state-of-the-art techniques. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/zwang84/DPVRD. When using this code, please cite this paper as follows: Z. Wang, Y. Zhang, J. Zhang, and C. Zhang, "Dual-Phase Visual Relationship Detection," arXiv preprint arXiv:2005.02425 (2020). Additionally, we have incorporated two new evaluation metrics known as AP50+1 and CAR that provide a relationship between the detection accuracy and the level of false positives. These metrics demonstrate DPVRD's effectiveness in reducing false positives at a reasonable cost in terms of missing actual relationships. Our analysis indicates that DPVRD is particularly efficient in eliminating erroneous positive relationships that arise from the incorrect connection of two objects that do not possess a relationship. We believe our work contributes significantly to the further development of the Visual Relationship Detection field. In order to achieve this, we will continue improving DPVRD and making the updated code publicly available on GitHub. This study offers a supervised action recognition solution, known as Delta Sampling R-BERT, capable of identifying human actions from video sequences. Delta Sampling R-BERT utilizes a unique frame selection method called Delta Sampling, which chooses frames to analyze based on their unique distance from neighboring frames. This approach ensures that the model focuses on frame movements rather than stationary positions. By incorporating these selected frames into a part-based R-BERT framework, Delta Sampling R-BERT achieves notable improvements in action recognition accuracy, particularly on limited and low-light datasets. Experimental results show that our proposed method outperforms existing methods on low-light action recognition and matches or surpasses top-performing methods on restricted action recognition datasets. Furthermore, Delta Sampling R-BERT demonstrates practical applications in real-world scenarios through the integration of a simple data augmentation technique. A pivotal issue arises when a court compels an individual or a company to decrypt encrypted data. Opponents argue that this demand violates the First Amendment by implying the expression of a specific view or opinion, whereas proponents see it as a reasonable request to recover already possessed information in a readable form. Previous analyses of this problem have been extensively reviewed, along with some novel cryptographic solutions to address it. A new framework is introduced, offering a broader perspective on the problem through the lens of game theory. Essentially, the government's decryption compulsion can be seen as an insecure multi-party computation (MPC) problem, where already controlling the answer is equivalent to an unconditional victory for the government. Various scenarios represent distinct security levels for the compressor, ranging from honest-but-curious compressors with limited computing power to highly malicious compressors with unlimited computing power. A notable solution is found for an ideal compressors model, where the compressor possesses the capacity for any computational task. Additionally, an analysis of the Computationally Honest Compressor (CHC) model is conducted, where the compressor's computing power is limited to some specific function, allowing for an optimal solution under particular conditions, although no solution is found for unconditional security. Nonetheless, this framework contributes a novel perspective to this problem, potentially informing future policy discussions. Some novel solutions are presented for specific cases, rather than the general case of an infinite set of compressors. Specifically, a secure decryption compulsion is achievable when there are multiple compressors, one for each user, assuming each compressor acts in an individually honest-but-curious manner and where the computing power of these compressors is limited to some specific function, or when there is one compressor, assuming this compressor acts in an openly non-collusive manner. No secure decryption compulsion exists for any compressor that engages in covert non-collusion. Additionally, some existing solutions such as the rule of 'know what you are compromising' can be re-interpreted through this framework, where this rule represents a situation where the compressor's pre-condition is implicit, thus no explicit contract can be written, thus this compels the court to ensure that the compressors are actually trustworthy. Lastly, this framework can be applied to address other encryption-related issues, such as key-escrow systems, where some of these solutions can be considered as variants of secure decryption compulsion. We introduce an infinite family of integers, labeled by combinatorial sequences, that remains invariant under a specific homotopy equivalence. This equivalence is defined by a set of rules based on the properties of partitional generating functions. By applying and extending earlier work by Tzanov and Sherratt, we demonstrate that this invariance predicts a particular distribution of partitional elements among the integers. As a result, we derive a general formula for calculating the sum of all partitional elements with a specific distribution. Consequently, we are able to express the Euler characteristic of a specific family of simplicial complexes, known as ordered set partitions, using this formula. The associated data, comprising combinations of combinatorial sequences, forms the basis of a higher-dimensional generalization of the Euler characteristic. Furthermore, we establish a direct connection between the integers and this higher-dimensional generalization, revealing its underlying structure. Ultimately, we identify a specific instance of the integers corresponding to the homotopy type of a celestial sphere in $n$-dimensional space. This connection also enables us to explore and interpret the results of computer simulations using a self-repelling system, and we are able to compare these findings with the predicted outcomes based on the integers. As part of this analysis, we introduce the concept of a locally unique configuration and show that it underlies both the self-repelling system and a related process known as a sandpile. Furthermore, we demonstrate that it plays a crucial role in determining the homotopy type of a celestial sphere. Additionally, we are able to generalize the integers to a broader framework that can be applied to both discrete and continuous domains. This generalization preserves the core properties of the original integers, including their relationship to homotopy types and self-repelling systems. As a result, this new framework can be used to answer any question about the homotopy type of a celestial sphere in $n$-dimensional space. This solution is a generalization of previous approaches and yields a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying structure of the integers. Recent research has focused on combining quantum nonlocality with unextendible product bases (UPBs) in multiple systems. However, most UPBs in various dimensions do not display nonlocality. A novel approach has been found to consistently identify subsets of UPBs exhibiting robust quantum nonlocality throughout various dimensions. Using this approach, a vast number of instances of nonlocal UPBs have been found in 3-dimensional systems and a significant number in 4-dimensional systems. Moreover, this approach has facilitated the creation of local operations and classical communications (LOCC) transformers, enabling the conversion of any UPB in a 3-dimensional system into another that has nonlocality. Yet, this capability does not extend to LOCC in 4-dimensional systems. To achieve this understanding, a series of entanglement measures have been explored and found particularly useful in analyzing nonlocal UPBs. Notably, one such measure has been found to closely resemble a well-known entanglement measure when the systems involved are identical, offering further insight into the nonlocality of UPBs. To broaden the scope of nonlocal UPBs, a novel principle has been proposed, enabling the identification of such bases in any combination of 3-dimensional systems. Through application of this principle, several nonlocal UPBs have been found in 3-dimensional systems consisting of up to 5 subsystems. A significant breakthrough has been achieved in 4-dimensional systems, where a fundamental limitation has been identified, defining the minimum number of 4-dimensional systems required to support a nonlocal UPB. Furthermore, this breakthrough has demonstrated that any UPB in a 4-dimensional system can be transformed into another that has nonlocality via LOCC in that same dimension. This research extensively expands our knowledge of nonlocal UPBs and offers a novel understanding of quantum nonlocality across multiple systems. It also provides a valuable framework for identifying and analyzing such phenomena through the use of entanglement measures. As a result, this research will contribute significantly to the advancement of quantum information science. With its diverse applications spanning cryptography, communication, and metrology, a deeper understanding of nonlocal UPBs will be crucial in developing many future quantum technologies. Furthermore, this research will provide a foundation for exploring even more complex quantum systems, enabling us to better comprehend the intricate relationships between quantum nonlocality, entanglement, and UPBs in multiple systems. As a result, our method becomes a powerful tool for selecting models and estimating parameters in large-scale, complex datasets consisting of continuous and categorical variables. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. Next steps will involve a comparative analysis of our data with other observations of our targets to derive a more comprehensive understanding, in addition to expanding our study to more distant galaxies that are undergoing mergers. Additionally, we aim to utilize our data to model the evolution of gas outflow with merger phase, and to explore whether this outflow pattern holds true for all galaxy mergers as seen with our team's study. Furthermore, we will utilize our results to submit a proposal for even higher resolution optical/near-infrared IFU observations of our targets with the Seimei Telescope, as well as for X-ray observations of our targets with the X-ray Observatory with a focus on active supermassive black holes and the outflow of gas. Achieving high performance on diverse datasets through a single machine learning model is challenging due to its limitations in simultaneously achieving optimal performance across multiple objectives. To overcome this, transferring knowledge from one model to another is a widely adopted strategy. However, existing methods require shared representation spaces for the source and target models, which can be restrictive. In this study, we introduce a novel approach to zero-shot knowledge transfer between black-box models whose internal workings are not accessible. By leveraging decision-based data from the source model, we enable zero-shot knowledge transfer for target models representing any possible function within the given dataset. We facilitate this transfer by generating a new model that accurately predicts the source model's decisions, which in turn enables us to find a model for the target task that accurately replicates the data from the source model. We validate our approach through comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over baseline models and showcasing the potential for zero-shot learning on unseen datasets. We investigate the computational complexity of a robust version of the geodetic
problem, which can be represented as a graph problem known as $K_t$ clique detection.
The standard geodetic problem is equivalent to finding the largest subset of a graph's vertices that forms a $K_t$ clique. A specific subset of vertices is considered robust for this problem if it satisfies particular condition and cannot be overwhelmed by the graph's other vertices. The target is to determine the largest robust subset of vertices that forms a $k$-element $K_t$ clique. We provide a proof that this problem has a highest known complexity of NP when the number of vertices in the graph is fixed, which represents an incomplete proof of a conjecture made by F. F. Dragan and S. S. Yannakou. Additionally, we present a framework that indicates this problem has a highest known complexity of CH when the number of vertices in the graph is part of the problem's input parameters. This framework is relevant to a broader category of graph problems known as minimal domain problem. We also provide a proof that a particular variant of this problem can be solved efficiently when a subset of the graph's vertices forms a $K_t$ clique with a specific property, which is described as the "strong" property. This proof is relevant to an earlier study made by F. F. Dragan and S. S. Yannakou. The success of imitation learning relies heavily on an optimal expert policy being available for supervision. Yet, obtaining expert demonstrations is often hindered by difficulties in scaling and synthesizing high-quality actions. As a result, there's a need to develop algorithms that can efficiently learn from non-expert data, leveraging existing knowledge only if it's beneficial. We introduce the problem of low-quality expert data and propose the TRAIL framework, which learns from a mixture of high-quality but limited labeled data and low-quality but abundant unlabeled data. We demonstrate on real-world tasks, including complex games and real-world workflows, that our TRAIL algorithm leveraging non-expert data successfully outperforms baseline methods. Interestingly, we find that using subpar expert data can still yield better performance than not using it, highlighting the potential for imitation learning to make use of existing knowledge. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation algorithm to circumvent this issue. Co-Imitation leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation algorithm, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Notably, Co-Imitation achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art joint reinforcement and imitation learning methods while requiring no common action space or reward space. Moreover, we explore the implications of varying inter-agent distance on performance and provide a qualitative analysis of successful imitation cases. The code for our novel Co-Imitation algorithm is publicly available online. In this research, we demonstrate that by incorporating a linear layer after the final fully connected layer of the source sentence encoder, reversible transformations of any source sentences can be generated, making it feasible to use reinforcement learning for neural machine translation. Our proposed method achieves notable improvements in data efficiency and produces novel sentence generations for the training dataset without additional cost. Moreover, our approach allows for the generation of multiple possible outputs for each source sentence and does not face the difficulty of directly learning action embeddings from the action space, as is the case with multi-head attention in neural machine translation models. Our experiments show that this proposed method achieves significant gains in performance when compared to the baseline models, particularly in low-resource settings and when translating between highly similar languages. Our results also indicate that the linear layer and reversible transformations play a crucial role in the performance improvements. To handle large action spaces, our proposed method is further expanded to use linear transformations for both source and target sentence embeddings, leading to improved performance on semantic tasks such as sentiment analysis and commodity classification. Our research provides evidence that neural machine translation models can benefit from linear transformations and reversible transformations, however further studies are needed to fully understand the implications and potential solutions to this issue. In this research, we develop an innovative technique for a robot's depth camera to determine its optimal positioning and orientation in relation to a target object, using information from a virtual point cloud obtained from the robot's surroundings. This approach bypasses the need for object markers, enabling its application to everyday items with diverse shapes and textures. The development of this technique involves training a virtual pose estimation model, which can predict the ideal camera positioning and end-effector pose to grasp the object, based on a point cloud that reflects the actual environment. To achieve this, a markerless setting is created to obtain a point cloud from the depth camera, allowing the extraction of a two-dimensional template from a specific depth range. The template and surrounding environment are then used to calculate the object's pose, which in turn facilitates training and evaluation of the deep learning-based pose estimation model. The proposed system's performance shows promising results, with an average accuracy of 3.25 millimeters in estimating the end-effector pose, following optimization of the camera settings and setting the tolerance for pose similarity to 0.04 radians. A rational number p/q is considered identifiable if its denominator q is minimal among all equivalent fractions representing the same value. The current leading medical image analysis models are based on deep learning techniques and strive to provide personalized care by classifying medical images into specific patient groups.  Despite the tremendous potential, these models face a significant hurdle in overcoming inherent biases present in their training datasets.  In this research, we introduce a novel framework that simultaneously detects biases and improves the performance of image classification.  This framework is comprised of two main components:  the first identifies data imbalances by detecting rare image regions and distinguishing them from common ones;  the second corrects these biases by generating new balanced datasets through rare region enhancement.  Our experimental results on multiple medical image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our bias identification framework, with a notable increase in classification accuracy after bias correction.  Specifically, our model achieves a notable 8% improvement in differential diagnosis of breast biopsies, 23% improvement in identifying diabetic macular edema, and 5% improvement in detecting skin cancer.  We believe this research will contribute significantly to the development of unbiased medical image analysis models.  We have incorporated multiple forms of bias into skin cancer datasets and demonstrated the potential of our framework to remedy them, resulting in enhanced cancer detection performance.  We have also explored the potential of transfer learning to handle diabetic retinopathy datasets and showed that our framework is effective in identifying and rectifying biases in limited labeled dataset scenarios.  We have made our datasets and implementation publicly available on GitHub.  We have further investigated the potential of unsupervised rare region detection and found that our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques by a significant margin, with an ROCAOPC score of 0.18 over the base model, primarily due to the reduction of intrinsic bias, thereby enabling efficient rare region enhancement using a limited number of labeled samples.  We have also explored the application of our bias identification framework to medical text classification, with promising early results, and we have formed a new research direction focused on uncovering biases in medical datasets through rare region detection.  We have become members of the Medical Biometrics Society and have initiated a new research direction named "Biometrics for Biases".  We have expressed our concerns on the inherent biases present in medical datasets and associated challenges to renowned medical biometrics experts and renowned medical specialists. The results it produces include quantitative data on biases' statistical characteristics, power spectra, and specific forecasted recovery coefficients for standard cosmological parameters. In the past, programmers had to utilize the natural cycles of mechanical devices such as clock hands, spinning tops, and motorized balls to create simulations. In the 1940s and early 1950s, researchers like John von Neumann and others began incorporating artificial time steps into their simulations, referring to the process as 'timestepping'. However, the concept of storing intermediate simulation results on magnetic tape or disk was first explored in the 1940s and wasn't widely adopted until the 1950s and 1960s. We've conducted an in-depth analysis of the Forsage cryptocurrency program, often described as a pyramid scheme, and explored its underlying mechanisms to understand why it has been successful in deceiving victims globally. By examining the program's design and tracking its transactions on the Ethereum blockchain, we uncovered a complex sequence of transactions known as an "abundance ring" that the developers likely created to evade detection by exchange operators who monitor and prevent activities associated with pyramid schemes and money laundering. Through a survey of 1500 active Forsage participants, we gained insight into the appeal of the program to its users and identified key aspects of the abundance ring that contribute to its resilience. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the Forsage scheme has an extremely robust and self-sustaining feature that has enabled it to continue operating freely on the blockchain. This research can contribute to the development of more effective strategies for identifying and preventing the emergence of similar deception schemes on blockchains. Additionally, our findings may aid in informing educational programs aimed at promoting digital literacy and safe online investment practices. By combining these efforts, we can work together to mitigate the harm caused by these types of deception schemes and other malicious activities on blockchains. We investigated 19 red clump and horizontal branch candidate stars within the Milky Way's bulge using data from the VVV survey. By determining their magnitudes and assessing surrounding crowd levels, we established proper motions for the proposed globular clusters and compared them to existing maps of the bulge's structure, ultimately identifying their locations. However, we were unable to confirm any of the 19 candidate globular clusters, with 14 being linked to known open or globular clusters, while the remainder correspond to small groups of stars. Furthermore, we established a list of potential cluster candidates, with 5 showing distinct features on color-magnitude diagrams, and suggested follow-up observations to verify their status as globular clusters. Additionally, we provided estimates for the density and mass of two previously undiscovered open clusters within the bulge.

Current implementations rely on an auxiliary classifier, which hinders the model's sparsity potential. To address this limitation, we present SparseGAN, a novel sparsifiable Generative Adversarial network, in which the generator and critic are trained through a multi-task approach. The generator is trained using a noise vector, promoting sparsity, while the critic is trained to classify the generated text as real or fake. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on several sparsity-inducing text generation tasks, according to metrics such as sentence embedding sparseness, local sparseness, and diversity. Notably, the embeddings produced by SparseGAN outperform those of the state-of-the-art dense model on eight out of nine tasks. Our model's effectiveness is further demonstrated through unsupervised classification and clustering experiments, indicating that sparse text generation leads to more efficient representation of semantic structures and patterns. This study proposes a technique for independent situational awareness in swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles. The method enables each drone to analyze its surroundings independently, using its own sensors and a nearby cluster of neighbor drones, without the need for a central controller. This approach is tested in a simulated environment and the results show that the independent situation awareness algorithm allows the swarm to detect a red object in 5.6 seconds, compared to 7.2 seconds for a centrally controlled swarm. Additionally, the independent approach detects the red object when the drone is farther away from it. This technique has potential applications in swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles used in surveillance, search and rescue operations, and detecting red objects. Recent discoveries of an abnormal Nernst effect in magnetic materials near their transition points have renewed interest in understanding the spin-dependent thermal transport. A specific class of antiferromagnetic materials, known as the Heusler compounds, exhibits unique magnetic properties that could harbor this abnormal Nernst effect. However, extensive research on these materials is necessary to fully elucidate the relationship between their magnetic structure and spin-dependent thermal transport. In this study, we investigate the spontaneous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN Heusler films, examining how different magnetic structures influence spin-dependent thermal transport. These films exhibit unusual Nernst coefficients that can be both positive and negative, depending on the magnitude of the applied magnetic field. Notably, we find that the unusual Nernst effect is closely linked to the scattering of electrons by magnetic defects, and we demonstrate this connection by conducting a thermal transport study in epitaxial Mn$_3$GaN films, which have significantly fewer magnetic defects and thus display much smaller unusual Nernst effects. By incorporating magnetic defects, however, we are able to enhance the unusual Nernst effect to the same magnitude as that observed in the Mn$_3$NiN films using a thin layer of Mn$_3$NiN on top of the Mn$_3$GaN substrate. This finding has significant implications for the design of devices that utilize the unusual Nernst effect, suggesting that incorporating materials with magnetic structures is crucial for optimizing these devices. Moreover, we believe that this work will contribute significantly to the ongoing research in the spin-dependent thermal transport of materials. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the value of a combination of theoretical and experimental research in achieving a comprehensive understanding of the unusual Nernst effect. In particular, we utilized both empirical and tight-binding models to analyze the electronic structure and magnetic properties of these materials. Our research on the unusual Nernst effect has also sparked interest in examining the spin-Hall effect in these materials, and we plan to investigate this phenomenon further in the future. Additionally, we would like to study the unusual Nernst effect in these materials under different temperatures and magnetic conditions, and investigate the possibility of enhancing this effect by adjusting the composition of these materials. Our study has already generated significant interest in the research community, and we look forward to continuing this work in the future. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian with rapid dynamic changes and a problem Hamiltonian with slower changes that represent the problem to be solved. Successful outcome relies on driver Hamiltonians that maintain non-stoquastic properties, yet this seems contradictory since stoquastic Hamiltonians are generally required to prevent thermal bias and ensure the efficacy of quantum annealing. Our research reveals that, in fact, driver Hamiltonians with strong anti-ferromagnetic interactions always lead to catastrophic failures in quantum annealing, causing isolated systems to result in an instantaneous ground state upon rapid driver Hamiltonian transformation. This devastating consequence arises from an unnatural path in quantum dynamics, which can be transformed into a natural path by incorporating environmental influences such as photon field decoherence. Our findings suggest that quantum annealing only achieves its intended goal when driver Hamiltonians have very weak non-stoquastic properties or, more generally, when they exhibit diverse types of coupling. Furthermore, even mild driver Hamiltonian imperfections can cause catastrophic failures, implying the necessity of precisely controlling both problem and driver Hamiltonians. These conclusions demonstrate the significance of accounting for both perfect problem Hamiltonian and precise driver Hamiltonian in the success of quantum annealing. Our research also introduces a novel criterion for driver Hamiltonians that can prevent disastrous failures, which can be validated through imaginary time dynamics instead of full-scale quantum annealing simulations. This criterion, coupled with quantum circuit learning, can select the most suitable driver Hamiltonians from a vast variety of possibilities, essentially eliminating the risk of catastrophic failures in quantum annealing. As a result, we are able to successfully execute the maximum bias scenario even with driver Hamiltonians that exhibit substantial, uncompromising non-stoquastic properties. Our innovations have the potential to greatly expand the capabilities of quantum annealing to solve complex problems under a wide range of imperfect conditions. These breakthroughs can be achieved through the integration of quantum learning, coupled with both exact and approximate versions of our new driver Hamiltonian criteria, which can fundamentally transform the landscape for solving difficult problems using quantum annealing. Furthermore, our findings imply that quantum annealing will likely face significant challenges when applied to fundamental research problems that involve observing actual ground state properties, such as the spontaneous emission rate or the geometric phase, which are embedded in extensive Hamiltonians and, therefore, have extensive non-stoquastic properties. Additionally, we explored how to effectively use these predictions to control a robotic leg to mimic the individuals' own step rates. The unique blend of decentralization and pseudo-anonymity in blockchain-based cryptocurrencies has made them appealing for both legitimate use cases and illicit activities. Due to the relatively small size of individual cryptocurrency transactions, a combination of low-value transactions or repeated transfers (known as mixers) can successfully conceal the identities of criminals and obscure the detection of illicit funds. In an effort to combat these issues, our research focuses on the development of an advanced technique for identifying and tracing cryptocurrency transactions that involve suspicious activities such as money laundering, terrorist financing, and malicious mining. By leveraging the benefits of graph theory and artificial intelligence, our proposed method depicts the blockchain network as a dynamic graph of interconnected nodes, where the identification of suspicious activities is determined by the detection of certain patterns within this graph. Our results, derived from the analysis of the Bitcoin blockchain between 2018 and 2020, reveal the presence of illicit transactions in all examined periods and highlights the effectiveness of our proposed approach in tracing certain transactions. Furthermore, our analysis provides valuable insights into the temporal and currency-independent characteristics of the blockchain network, shedding light on the permanent existence of malicious actors within the blockchain community. Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Notably, supporting employees' inherent needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness is crucial in the remote working context. Our findings indicate that both home working and Scrum use contribute to project success, with Scrum playing a mediating role. Furthermore, both work-related and personal factors influence an individual's ability to thrive in both Scrum and home working environments, which we refer to as'sweet spots'. The theoretical framework proposes several'sweet spots' where an individual's needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness are met, leading to enhanced project success and overall well-being. This research contributes to both the Scrum and home working literatures by providing empirical evidence and a comprehensive theoretical framework. It highlights the importance of'sweet spots' and presents several practical guidelines for both Scrum practitioners and managers. Furthermore, it proposes several areas for future research. This research is unique in that it addresses the gap in Scrum research by exploring the influence of home working on Scrum project success and identifies several'sweet spots' that enhance both project success and well-being. It is also one of the first studies on home working and Scrum that gathers data from a sample of software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our study investigates the underlying causes of elliptic flow coefficient asymmetry as seen in final particle spectra from the ALICE detector in the Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV.  Based on a collective motion model that relates the initial energy density to the final particle distribution, we manipulate the event shape of the ALICE sample events by increasing the influence of elliptical and triangular anisotropies.  Our findings show that the increased elliptical anisotropy in the sample events results in higher than expected elliptic flow coefficient values, while triangular anisotropy has little effect.  Furthermore, our research demonstrates that manipulated events with the same anisotropy mix as observed in the ALICE data still exhibit higher than expected elliptic flow coefficient values for particles with intermediate momenta.  Our study also reveals that the cross-over behavior between elliptical and triangular anisotropies in the data could be a consequence of the anisotropy mix, rather than a specific property of the quark-gluon plasma.  Finally, our research suggests that the overpopulation of particles in the intermediate momentum range in the ALICE data may be a related phenomenon, as it persists in manipulated events that match the anisotropy mix of the ALICE data.  Additionally, we investigate how the influence of radial flow affects this interpretation, while incorporating measurements from the CMS detector.  Our study paves the way for further investigation of transverse momentum anisotropies and related phenomena in the ALICE and CMS detectors.  We anticipate that forthcoming data from the CMS detector, which includes charged hadron measurements, will provide greater insight into this aspect of heavy ion collisions.  Our study demonstrates that the event shape manipulation technique offers a unique approach for exploring the anisotropic nature of heavy ion collisions through the spectrum-and-flow correlation, an unexplored aspect of this research field.  This study is an essential step for more intricate event shape manipulation techniques that will be applied to forthcoming data from the ALICE and CMS detectors, which will investigate middle momentum anisotropies in heavy ion collisions.  We anticipate that such techniques will be applicable not only to heavy ion collisions but also to high-energy proton-proton collisions, allowing a deeper understanding of the underlying causes of flow coefficient asymmetry in heavy ion collisions.  As a result, this study will provide a valuable framework for further investigation of the event shape manipulation technique on flow coefficient asymmetry in heavy ion collisions, including forthcoming data from the ALICE and CMS

This paper examines the extreme gains achieved by optimal power control in comparison to binary (on/off) power control in interference networks with multiple users. We demonstrate that the proportion of gains realizable through binary power control reaches its maximum value of $\Omega(\sqrt{K})$ as the number of users increases, to an infinitesimally small degree of precision. Furthermore, this ratio of gains consistently surpasses the theoretical maximum achievable through binary power control by a quantity of at least $\Omega(\sqrt{K})$. We derive this maximum achievable binary power control gain as $0.5\Omega(\sqrt{K})$. As a result, in networks with large numbers of users, the gains provided by optimal power control over binary power control can be substantial. We achieve this optimal ratio of gains through a generalization of a previously developed strategy and validate our results numerically. We also present an approximation for binary power control gains that holds true with an error of less than one hundredth of a decibel and is derived from measurements of actual networks. This finding is relevant to the design of on/off power control systems due to their widespread use in a variety of applications. We introduce a new notation for describing multi-user interference networks and a new formula for sum capacities, both of which may be useful tools for future research. This study introduces an alternative integration approach for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional methods can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration method utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional methods. Our method was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our method reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$. We demonstrate that the general form of such congruences, given the constraint that $a$ and $b$ remain relatively prime, can be represented as the sum of two perfect squares, namely $a^2+(a+b)^2$. This expression is equivalent to a value of $7$ raised to a power of $n$, where $n$ is a whole number. Furthermore, we show that any solution to this type of congruence, under the condition that $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime, has a corresponding form which involves the use of congruence classes, specifically in the form of $a \equiv 1 \mod{7}$ and $b \equiv -1 \mod{7}$. We explore two methods of proof. Firstly, we utilize a form of induction which allows us to arrive at a specific expression for any positive integer $n$. Secondly, we utilize a method which can be described as follows: having established the base case for the exponent $n=1$, we then demonstrate that if the congruence holds true for a particular value of $n$, it is also true for $2n$. This is achieved by manipulating the variables $a$ and $b$ in such a way that we can derive the form of the expression for $2n$ from the form of the expression for $n$. This enables us to conclude that the congruence is true for all positive integers $n$. Finally, we provide examples of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ results in values of $7$ raised to a power of $n$, where $n$ is a whole number in the range from $1$ to $4$. Additionally, we discuss the implications of this analysis in relation to further general congruences, specifically those which involve expressions which can be factored as the difference of two perfect squares, as well as considerations regarding moduli which are based on the square of a prime number. This analysis may provide a useful framework for addressing more general congruences in the field of number theory. This article concludes with an open-ended problem

However, this very same screening that influences the nickelate's electronic structure also gives rise to a counter-effective effect on superconductivity, ultimately requiring a delicate balance to favor superconducting onset. Our theoretical framework also facilitates an explanation for superconductivity's incompatibility with antiferromagnetic ordering, by showing that long-range magnetic ordering hinders the necessary screening by pushing the oxygen electrons out of reach. This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By analyzing the underlying dynamical and coercive properties of the collision operator, we've demonstrated the existence of polynomial growth estimates on the linearized operator, resulting in the convergence to the equilibrium phase. Additionally, we've identified the optimal convergence rates under both symmetric and asymmetric collision conditions. Moreover, we've derived specific decay rates for initial data with smooth and compact support, yielding decay estimates on the convergence rate. Moreover, this study demonstrates the emergence of a blending phenomenon, where the long-term behavior is a combination of the initial data's smooth components and its compact support properties. Indeed, the convergence to equilibrium is achieved through the phase shift of the smooth components and the dispersion of the compact support region. This research provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation in an infinite space. Indeed, it reveals the intricate relationship between the dynamical and coercive properties of the collision operator, which is a critical component for guaranteeing the convergence to equilibrium. This study is a significant expansion of the authors' previous work on the simplified equation, which was conducted as part of the 2019-2020 research group on the Boltzmann equation at the University of Vienna. The current work builds upon this foundation with more elaborate collision conditions, which is an important advancement in the study of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation. This research will be presented at the 2022 European Mathematical Society (EMS) Workshop on Partial Differential Equations in Vienna, Austria. Yet, the discovery of larger than predicted interlayer magnetic penetration depths in these materials raised issues with the tunneling model's validity. The emergence of charge density wave states at low temperatures further compromised the tunneling model's applicability. This study seeks to address these concerns by enhancing the tunneling model to account for charge density oscillations between CuO planes, a function that can be implemented through the introduction of additional Josephson couplings. The modified model is capable of replicating the complex electronic properties observed in the cuprates, thus providing a theoretical framework that explains the relationship between spin density wave states, charge density oscillations, and superconductivity within these materials. The model also facilitates a representation of the London penetration depth as a sum of intralayer and interlayer components, a charge density that can vary with temperature and an effective interlayer superconducting gap. The proposed model offers a theoretical foundation for understanding the observed magnitude of interlayer magnetic penetration depths and the temperature-dependent behavior of the cuprates' magnetic susceptibility. The study also indicates that the overestimation of the tunneling depth is a result of the model's ability to model intralayer and interlayer superconductivity separately. The model's predictions are supported by the results of numerical simulations, based on the extended Foley-Hirschfeld-Gabayes model, that demonstrate how the introduction of Josephson couplings between layers can give rise to the formation of charge density oscillations, an observation that is further verified through the application of the Fukuyama-Shiba theory. The proposed model offers a more comprehensive theoretical description of the electronic properties of the cuprate materials, a description that can be used to assess the feasibility of implementing quantum phase transition protocols in these systems. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. This involves considering the intricate web of interactions formed by atoms in a dissipative two-dimensional fluid. Our approach showcases the value of unifying theoretical models and experimental techniques, such as bio-jump imaging, and highlights the capacity of graph neural networks to provide transparent and easily interpretable results. Through the exploration of artificial datasets, we validated the accuracy of our method in predicting critical phenomena and the reliability of its predictions in the face of significant distortions. Our research demonstrates that the proposed graph neural network paradigm offers a versatile tool for exploring complex phenomena on a microscopic scale, and it paves the way for the development of more intuitive, phenomenological theories that describe the processes involved. Furthermore, this approach may facilitate the identification of underlying processes in other situations where chaos arises, by providing a clearer, more detailed understanding of the phenomena through the visualization of low-dimensional manifolds. This understanding may be a key to addressing the broader question of how the complexity of chaotic phenomena arises from the combination of simple interactions between individual components. Our research demonstrates the value of a multi-faceted approach that integrates theoretical models, experimental techniques, and the development of interpretable models, and it shows that the proposed graph neural network paradigm is an effective tool for this kind of analysis. This approach may also facilitate the development of more transparent and easier to interpret models of complex phenomena that involve extensive connections and interactions, such as life, the development of diseases, and the behavior of economic systems, among others. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce performance by limiting bandwidth utilization. The proposed buffered asynchronous aggregation (BAA) framework overcomes this limitation by allowing devices to submit updates at any time, extending the concept to include devices that do not contribute to global aggregations. BAA introduces a computational challenge, significantly increasing the risk of converging to a saddle point or a local minimum. To address this, this research introduces a noise injection method called relaxed batched optimal asynchronous aggregation (RBOAA) and evaluates its performance against several baselines, showing that it can achieve comparable performance to synchronized federated learning for non-noisy data and significantly improve performance for low-quality updates. The study also examines the optimal selection of learning rates in BAA and presents a scalable, noise-free algorithm called full batch optimal asynchronous aggregation (FBOAA), which is mathematically proven to converge at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{KT} + (K/T)^{1.5})$. The proposed methods are thoroughly evaluated using real-world image classification datasets and demonstrate the effectiveness of BAA for cross-device federated learning with a large number of participating devices. The implementation of the proposed methods is also examined, showing the potential for optimized asynchronous optimization to be applied in other settings where restrictions on gradient updates are imposed. The study's results are of interest to academia and industry practitioners working on federated learning and optimized computation for cross-device settings. A novel algorithm for precise force control in series elastic actuators is introduced in this paper, centered on a cutting-edge force estimation technique called the transmission force observer. This approach was developed to enhance the inaccurate force readings caused by the nonlinear elastic transmission and sensor measurement errors of the actuators' deformation sensors. The study first critiques conventional SEA force sensing methods, examining their stochastic properties that ultimately enable accurate force control through the proposed transmission force observer. A critical parameter derived from system analysis is key in optimizing the performance of the force-controlled system, guiding the achievement of the optimal outcome. This developed algorithm is successfully validated using actual SEA hardware setup for its effectiveness. Key advantages of the proposed algorithm include its capability to handle a wide range of system parameters, as well as its simplicity and minimal reliance on precise knowledge of the system parameters, making it suitable for a variety of application scenarios. In the context of allocating essential goods to self-interested agents who engage in competitive behavior, we aim to identify a fair distribution that holds across all conceivable equilibria in a game. We have developed a general framework for achieving this goal in scenarios where goods can be divided, based on the Max-Total-Value (MTV) principle, which ranks preferences according to the overall value obtained by each agent. When divisibility is possible, we can find a fair equilibrium through a direct approach. However, when goods must be allocated entire, we propose an auction mechanism that ensures the existence of a fair equilibrium for any number of agents. This mechanism involves a series of secondary auctions, conducted one good at a time, where the available quantity serves as the payment term. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this mechanism by showing that it produces a pure Nash equilibrium and fair outcomes for each agent. Furthermore, we examine special cases, including the scenario of described preferences, uncertain valuations with known distributions, and the allocation of divisible goods. Building on these results, we explore additional questions for future research. When goods must be divided, we established fair allocations in pure Nash equilibria in accordance with the MTV rule. For auctions without information, we found a crucial constraint that prevents the existence of a fair equilibrium. Investigating the case of divisible goods through the lens of auction without information, we discovered a new connection to the concept of fair individual allocations. We defined a robust and efficient mechanism for allocating divisible goods that produces a fair equilibrium and optimal social welfare as a result of efficient auction without information. This research is a continuation of the study on allocation of indivisible goods first introduced by Kelso and Crawford (1982) and provides a new answer to the question posed by that paper. Our research focuses on leveraging paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. We examined two aspects of this experiment: the requirements for detecting nuclear hits caused by dark matter and the necessary detection rates of cosmogenic neutrons. We established that paleo-detectors can successfully identify dark matter with a mass of one george (approximately 10^-26 eV) if it comprises 27% of the universe's mass density. Our findings also revealed that detecting nuclear hits caused by dark matter is more sensitive to the experiment's sensitivity to cosmogenic neutrons than any other factor. This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-like spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the infinitesimal generator of phi for the semigroup [phi_t, BMOA_p] to equal VMOA_p. We also establish the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the Volterra-type operators T_g, specifically examining which symbols g make T_g bounded or compact from BMOA to BMOA_1, while also investigating the relationship between compactness and weak compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2. Additionally, we establish the compactness of the integral operators with continuous symbols on VMOA_1, extending a result of M. Kawada and T. Kawada. Finally, we provide a characterisation of the compact operators on BMOA_1 that have a representation as an integral operator with a symbol in the Lipschitz space Lip(1/2,1/2). This analysis also extends to the space VMOA_1. Our proof of the compactness of T_g for continuous symbols g also relies on a more general result involving the compactness of composition operators on BMOA_1, which follows from examining the semigroups of composition operators and Volterra operators on BMOA_1.

To overcome this, we propose an innovative LSTM memory cell structure called HT-LSTM that utilizes the low-rank tensor decomposition to significantly reduce memory usage while maintaining high accuracy performance. By combining this probe with x-ray absorption spectroscopy, researchers have introduced a new technique called nuclear stage retrieval spectroscopy (NRS). NRS can determine the properties of nuclear states by analyzing the retrieved x-ray emission following x-ray absorption, albeit with the restriction that the initial x-ray absorption stage must contain significant contributions from multiple initial nuclear states. Nevertheless, NRS offers a useful complementary approach for studying nuclear states, particularly when employed in conjunction with x-ray free-electron lasers that allow for the selective creation of initial stages with differing nuclear configurations. This review introduces the principles of x-ray laser spectroscopy, describes the NRS technique, and explores its applications using both narrow-band and broad-band x-ray lasers. A numerical model is also presented to facilitate the interpretation of NRS spectra. The review concludes with an examination of the technical specifications required for x-ray lasers necessary for achieving accurate NRS measurements. A hybridized version of this method allows us to bypass the necessity of exact integration by part, instead using static condensation to solve for the pressure variable. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. This dataset is distinct from datasets used in classification tasks that rely on predictors of specific indicators, such as the Discourse Prediction Dataset. By changing the swimmer body and its helical tail dimensions, our findings reveal that viscoelastic properties' influence on swimming speed is particularly sensitive to the swimmer's front-to-back shape.  When this shape is broad, viscoelastic fluids actually slow the swimmer, whereas a more compact shape yields a viscoelastic-induced swimming speed boost.  To gain insight, we develop a theoretical viscoelastic fluid model that demonstrates how helical swimmers' speed responds to varying fluid properties and geometry. This analysis suggests that viscoelastic forces on swimmers can be either accelerated or delayed due to their helical tail's shape, which is influenced by the swimmer's asymmetry. This research provides a framework for analyzing more complex swimmers and their interaction with viscoelastic fluids. Furthermore, by controlling swimmer geometry, it is possible to manage the impact of viscoelastic forces, which has implications for swimmers that encounter a wide range of fluid conditions. Additionally, this study shows that both highly elastic and little elastic fluids result in similar swimmer speeds, indicating that there may be an optimal level of viscoelasticity that produces the best swimming performance. To confirm this, we examined even more intricate swimmers with multiple helical tails and discovered that this'sweet spot' viscoelasticity still applies, which could be useful in the development of swimmers for viscoelastic fluids. Approximately a decade ago, a computational framework centered on grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) emerged as a key component for spatial navigation within hippocampal network theories. This framework has undergone significant testing and his been found to withstand challenges posed by animal experiments. Recently, research has expanded beyond grid cells alone, examining other hippocampal neural networks that participate in the MEC. This survey discusses current understanding and various theories regarding neuron populations within the MEC, discussing their functions, underlying mechanisms, and the roles they play in generating grid cell behaviors. We discuss various grid cell types, such as flexible lattice cells, ring cells, and stationary cells, as well as the intrinsic properties of dorso-lateral grid cells, ambulatory grid cells, and grid cells that remain stable across sleep-wake cycles. We also explore the network mechanisms that may underlie these cell types, examining the implications of their discovery for computational models of navigation and the rings mechanism in particular, which may provide a solution to the scaling problem faced by grid cells. Finally, we discuss the open questions and challenges associated with the study of neuron networks within the MEC. We discuss current lattice reconstruction techniques, such as the method that utilizes double peak analysis to identify grid cell interferences, as well as the potential applications of machine learning to the study of grid cells. We also explore the challenges associated with scaling these studies to larger scales and the potential for advanced analytical techniques to reveal the functions of the hippocampal neural networks more clearly. We conclude by reviewing the progress that has been made in studying the MEC navigation networks and the opportunities that lie ahead in this field. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can either switch the laser pulse polarization or amplify it, depending on the waveplate's orientation. We provide numerical evidence supporting the feasibility of this idea and demonstrate its potential to efficiently utilize multi-petawatt laser pulses with high peak powers. This concept may also facilitate the creation of highly powerful, tightly focused laser beams with intensities exceeding $10^{23} \, \mathrm{W/cm^2}$. This could be particularly useful for very low-density target acceleration and probe light generation in extremely high-field environments. A preliminary assessment of this component's effectiveness is also presented, indicating that it can efficiently amplify linearly polarized light to more than 99% of the possible maximum value, while transforming circularly polarized light's initial low intensity into over 90% of its potential maximum intensity. This component's simplicity and robustness make it suitable for driving extremely powerful laser pulse applications in the most demanding environments. Furthermore, this technology may also be applicable across broad spectral ranges, from the far infrared to ultraviolet, by adjusting the waveplate's characteristics accordingly. This potential for wide spectral coverage, combined with the ability to efficiently utilize multi-petawatt laser pulses, makes this type of plasma waveplate a valuable tool for a wide range of cutting-edge applications. We believe that this new type of plasma waveplate will provide a crucial path for the development of future high-power laser facilities that can effectively tap the full potential of these powerful pulse sources. This technology has been made available for public access, and further development of this concept is now available for collaboration. As the field of high-power laser electronics continues to evolve, it is essential to monitor the progress of this work closely. We anticipate that this new type of plasma waveplate will play a key role in the development of future high-power laser facilities that can efficiently utilize the full potential of these powerful pulse sources. We would like to invite researchers to collaborate on further developing this concept, which holds great promise for the field of high-power laser electronics. With the ability to efficiently process multi-petawatt laser pulses, this type of plasma waveplate may also enable the creation of higher-intensity proton beams and more accurate proton therapy

This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. In field-free areas, the associated X-ray rays that miss the sensor can be steered in the direction of the LE mirror's symmetry line. Within the confines of a mirror-to-sensor package, this setup allows for the use of just one small area of each LE mirror. Furthermore, this arrangement prevents image distortions that are inherent to conventional LE mirrors. Our calculations and simulations indicate that this design is capable of providing optimal performance in X-ray detection. A deep learning framework has been applied to investigate the significance of using the cosmic speed field in modeling the halo mass function. Simulation data without the cosmic speed field was used as input, and the output compared to measurements from the COLDFEAR code which models halo formation considering the cosmic velocity field. The results from this comparison show that ignoring the cosmic speed field leads to disparities in halo occupancy and conditional mass, especially for larger halos. Additionally, a comparison with the ZOWU code that models halo formation without consideration of the cosmic velocity field shows that the two have consistent outcomes, further emphasizing the influence of the cosmic speed field on halo formation. 

According to the findings, incorporating the cosmic velocity field results in more precise models of halo occupancy and conditional mass, with a 5 percent improvement in predicting massive halos and a 50 percent improvement in predicting halos with conditional mass greater than 10 times the mean. Furthermore, when comparing models that are consistent with the laws of gravity and dynamics, a difference in halo occupancy and conditional mass of factors of two and ten respectively arises from including the cosmic velocity field, implying that this field should be integrated in an accurate description of halo formation. 

In addition, a discussion on the implications of these findings for models that do not consider the cosmic velocity field field is presented. While such models may predict observable quantities accurately, they may not be suitable for use in models of structure formation and the formation of highly massive objects. Furthermore, due to the influence of the cosmic velocity field, models that do not consider it will not be invariant under changes in the universe's expansion history, which could be used to improve the accuracy of such models. 

Finally, an area for future research is proposed. A potential limitation of the results obtained is the use of numerical simulations to model the universe's evolution, which may not accurately capture the universe's dynamics, particularly when considering the cosmic velocity field's influence on halo formation. Therefore, integrating deep learning models with precision cosmological simulations could provide a more accurate understanding of the universe's structure and the formation of its objects.

Converting ancient musical scores from image to text form can be challenging, as many historical documents lack accompanying audio. Currently, most techniques used for this conversion require multiple steps and significant amounts of manually labeled data. To overcome these limitations, we've developed a novel method that utilizes a small amount of labeled data in conjunction with unlabeled audio files to automatically produce text transcriptions of musical scores. Our approach involves employing Convolutive NMF to extract fundamental frequency tracks from spectrogram representations of audio files, combining these representations with the text transcriptions using semi-supervised learning, and ultimately using these combined features to generate more accurate text transcriptions of unseen audio files. Through comprehensive experiments, our proposed system consistently outperformed existing state-of-the-art models, demonstrating substantial gains in musical note recognition accuracy. Furthermore, our method displayed superior performance when processing longer audio files, likely due to the ability of Convolutive NMF to capture prolonged fundamental frequency patterns. To facilitate further research, we've made publicly available a substantial dataset comprising annotated audio files derived from a wide range of historical musical score images. Our method's effectiveness was validated through a step-by-step analysis of its components' impact on performance.
