We have developed a new numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. Our numerical simulations for massive stars have revealed instabilities associated with relativistic convection, while applications to neutron stars have used a boundary condition that adheres to the equation of state across all possible densities. 

Our new formulation has been implemented in the computer code PRUster, and through this project, we have established that the methodology can handle a wide range of evolutionary processes and configurations, potentially expanding the scope of applications in the study of rotating stars. Furthermore, this new approach has demonstrated the potential to uncover hidden patterns in the behavior of rotating stars through close examination of the unique properties of each fluid element. 

We have also discovered a novel phenomenon in the evolution of rotating stars, where an unexpected shift in angular velocity distribution occurs during the development of a stellar envelope, leading to a temporary instability in the star's evolution. This newly identified phenomenon has been found to result from the distribution of angular velocity being governed by the equations of balance rather than the Euler equation itself, potentially holding implications for the modification of existing codes that utilize the Euler equation.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically extract data from visually complex documents is the time and resources needed to manually label data. To overcome this, we propose a novel technique called "Document Guided Layout (DGL)" that significantly reduces the amount of labeling required. DGL achieves this by leveraging the overall document layout to guide the model's performance, rather than relying on individual object labels. Our results show that DGL can reduce object detection errors by 57% and extraction precision errors by 43% on average, all while significantly cutting labeling costs. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the potential for near-human performance on visually complex document object detection and extraction tasks with much lower labeling expenses. These findings could positively impact domains like financial document analysis where labeling data is costly. Our technique, consisting of three key components, can be applied to a variety of layout models, as shown in our experiments using the popular Tesseract model. Overall, our study highlights the feasibility of developing high-performant visual document extraction models using less-expensive labeling methods. These results could also be relevant to other layout-based object detection tasks. In addition to presenting our results, we introduce the Document labeling4P (4P denoting Performance, Precision, Quality, and economy) metric, a new evaluation framework that considers multiple labeling metrics, which could be useful for assessing other labeling strategies. Our research is now available as an open-source repository, containing our implementation and documentation of the evaluation experiments conducted with multiple layout models on various financial document datasets. Our study paves the way for further research into efficient data labeling methods that could be applied to other complex data annotation tasks. Additionally, we explore potential future directions for reducing data labeling costs, along with possible future research topics and potential applications in different domains. Our study is an initial investigation into efficient data labeling methods and we plan on continuing this line of research in the future. In particular, we could investigate even more cost-effective data labeling methods with our technique, such as incorporating additional document-level labels, making use of existing annotated datasets, or integrating external knowledge sources. Our study could also serve as a starting point for the exploration of other complex data annotation tasks that could benefit from the proposed evaluation framework and efficient data labeling methods. In the future, we could examine even more layout-based object detection and extraction models with our technique, or expand the study to other natural language processing tasks that could benefit from the proposed evaluation framework and efficient data labeling methods. Our study could serve as a starting point for the exploration of other financial document analysis tasks

Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We discuss the implications of our results for future detector networks. The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the disparity in health outcomes and the early detection of health issues are closely linked. To inform and guide community-based intervention, it is essential to develop a predictive model that utilizes housing data to identify risk factors for maternal mortality. We introduce a novel data annotation technique called 'Housing Ontology Graph' to represent housing data's semantic meaning and facilitate the extraction of relevant information for model training. Furthermore, we develop a customized neural network framework that leverages graph representations to predict the risk of maternal mortality associated with housing conditions, demonstrating its efficacy through a housing-related maternal mortality risk prediction case study. Large-scale housing datasets pose significant challenges for machine learning models due to their large feature spaces, hidden biases, and noisy data. To address these issues, we propose a range of techniques such as feature selection, bias detection, and data cleaning to create a reliable and unbiased dataset. Our research showcases the potential of marker-based neural network models to handle complex, large-scale housing datasets and extract valuable insights for predicting maternal mortality. These models can be applied to a broad range of community-based risk prediction scenarios. Additionally, our dataset preprocessing approaches can be adapted for use with other machine learning models. Our implementation of a Housing Ontology Graph and a marker-based neural network model is now publicly available on GitHub. It can be applied to a broad range of community-based risk prediction scenarios that involve large-scale, complex data sets. The graph-based data representation and the marker-based neural network model provide a new framework for building reliable and unbiased machine learning models. This approach can be adapted for use with other machine learning models, such as tabular neural networks and decision trees. Our approach offers a new solution for the data challenges associated with housing data sets. For mobile robots to successfully navigate complex environments, having an effective navigation system is crucial. While mapping techniques like HiMap have shown promise, most existing approaches represent the environment using a flat grid structure, which can be detrimental if the robot encounters obstacles that impede navigation. To address this limitation, we propose HiTMap, a novel hierarchical topological map representation that enables robots to navigate in environments with physical barriers. HiTMap utilizes a two-layer structure, combining a local metric map for local navigation and a connected topological map for higher-level guidance. By integrating this dual-representation framework, we've achieved a significant improvement in navigation performance, and our results indicate a notable increase in success rates when navigating through unfamiliar areas. Our HiTMap system also compares favorably to other prominent navigation systems, demonstrating its efficacy. The code for our approach has been made publicly available on GitHub. The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval Agitive Language Detection Competition is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect aggressive language in social media posts, combining two methods: a dialect-based approach and a machine-learning approach. For the dialect-based method, we utilized pre-trained language models to identify aggressive language, before selecting the optimal model parameters through grid search. For the machine-learning method, we directly applied a range of pre-trained models to predict aggressive language, also selecting the optimal model through grid search. Our final submission combined the results of these approaches to produce the most effective aggressive language detection model. This paper presents the methods employed by the UM-IU@LING system and evaluates its performance in the competition. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that draws on parallels between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then demonstrate the feasibility of adapting sophisticated numerical methods from fluid dynamics to tackle the complexities arising from the renormalization group, specifically the appearance of non-analytic behavior. The source of cosmic rays with energies exceeding 10^20 eV remains a major puzzle in astrophysics. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time.  Our work is a significant step towards designing more effective learning technologies that recognize and respond to curiosity in collaborative learning settings and also paves the way for the development of computer support for other important cognitive and emotional skills. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for analyzing complex data behaviors and addressing numerous tasks like regression, classification, and signal processing. While Gaussian processes offer an effective way to model real-world phenomena, their conventional squared-exponential kernel-based approach often relies on questionable assumptions about homogeneous signal decay. A significant alternative is the Mat\'ern Gaussian process, which utilizes a smoother kernel that is theoretically justifiable for modeling deterministic data processes. However, existing implementations of the Mat\'ern Gaussian process are limited to their traditional Euclidean domain applications, such as weather prediction and material defect analysis. This work introduces novel Mat\'ern Gaussian process formulations adapted to graph domains, enabling data-driven learning and inference techniques. Specifically, this study provides innovative kernel designs compatible with random walk-based and diffusion-based graph kernels, as well as a framework for determining these kernels' hyperparameters via Bayesian approaches. In addition, this work is enhanced by an accompanying open-source Python library called PyMGP, which provides an accessible and unified framework for working with Mat\'ern Gaussian processes on graphs. Through extensive experiments and evaluations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed models and algorithms on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing the potential of Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to excel in various graph applications. As a result, this work paves the way for the application of Mat\'ern Gaussian processes in machine learning and signal processing within complex domain structures, such as graphs structured by temporal interdependencies. Finally, this study on Mat\'ern Gaussian processes is also a significant contribution to the broader field of Gaussian process research, addressing an often-overlooked aspect, namely the analysis of Gaussian processes on graphs. In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and suppress a coordinate population of harmful insects. This system consists of two variables: the population of nematodes and the population of target insects. By applying the technique of persistence analysis, which involves examining the asymptotic behaviour of the model, it is possible to identify the conditions under which the population of nematodes and the population of target insects exist over time and reach a stable equilibrium. Through the examination of the model's boundary, which represents the model's limiting cases, it is possible to establish the conditions under which the population of target insects is reduced or maintained at a stable equilibrium, which indicates the effectiveness of the model in eliminating the population of target insects. Additionally, through the examination of the model's interior, which represents the model's general cases, it is possible to establish the conditions under which the population of nematodes exists over time and reaches a stable equilibrium. By applying the technique of Hopf bifocal stability, which involves examining the local stability and frequency of the model, it is possible to identify the conditions under which the population of target insects is reduced or maintained at a stable equilibrium and to establish the frequency at which the model reaches a stable equilibrium. Overall, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of the model's conditions, stability, and frequency, which can be utilized to develop effective microbial pesticide production techniques. Furthermore, this study offers a framework for investigating other environmental systems that involve the elimination and suppression of population populations. Additionally, this study highlights the importance of accounting for the suppressing effect in model analysis, through the examination of a specific model, and ultimately contributes to the expansion of general theoretical results. Specifically, this study contributes to the extension of the global asymptotic stability result for the model and the examination of the condition under which the population of target insects is reduced or maintained at a stable equilibrium, which ultimately leads to the development of an optimal control technique for population control. Moreover, this study contributes to the expansion of the global asymptotic stability result for the model with multiple preserving measures and ultimately leads to the development of an optimal control technique for population control, which relies on the comparison principle. Furthermore, this study contributes to the expansion of the global asymptotic stability result for the model with an infinite population of target insects and ultimately leads to the development of an optimal control technique for population control, which relies on the comparison principle and the technique of Hopf bifocal stability.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus segmentation method capable of accurately detecting and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus segmentation for histopathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the mapping process into two distinct stages. The first stage involves a simple classification model that identifies image regions likely to contain nuclei based on their spatial location within the image. Subsequently, a second stage, which utilizes a U-Net based model, refines the identification by examining the within-region density and texture. By integrating these two stages, the W-net model demonstrates enhanced performance compared to baselines, showcasing its capability to detect and extract nuclei from images with complex backgrounds seamlessly. Furthermore, the model exhibits robust performance across diverse datasets, achieving a notable 0.084 percentage error rate in evaluation metrics, outperforming state-of-the-art competitors. The W-net model's superior performance is attributed to its ability to extract rich region-based features, a property that is also advantageous in nucleus extraction tasks that rely on density and texture characteristics. As a result, this model is ideally suited for detecting and extracting nuclei from histopathology images. In addition to cancer diagnosis, this model's effectiveness in detecting and extracting nuclei from images with complex backgrounds makes it a suitable solution for other applications as well. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of inhibiting NLRP3 activation, thereby potentially halting the pyroptotic cell death that follows. To investigate the underlying dynamics of this process, a mathematical model of a single SARS-CoV-2-infected cell has been developed. The model includes the host's key biochemical pathways and can simulate the cell's response to the virus and various treatments. Utilizing the model, several scenarios have been examined to understand how the timing of anti-inflammatory treatment, as well as the treatment's intensity, influence the cell's fate. The model also predicts how the virus's replication, the resulting cell death, and the release of inflammatory factors such as IL-1β are affected by these conditions. The research provides a foundation for further exploration of anti-inflammatory strategies in treating COVID-19 and other infectious diseases that trigger pyroptosis. The model has been made publicly available and can be downloaded at https://github.com/mbDesignGroup/NLRP3_model. The model consists of several sub-models, including a viral replication model, an NLRP3 inflammasome model, a pyroptosis model, and an anti-inflammatory treatment model. The model's reliability was verified by comparing its predictions with experimental data on how the anti-inflammatory medication, NLRP3 inhibitor, affects the release of IL-1β in monocytes infected with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. The model has also been applied to predict how different doses of two additional anti-inflammatory medications, GL-3 and COL-3, which are derived from the cathepsin D inhibitor, would affect IL-1β release in the same circumstances. The model's findings suggest that these medications could be effective in preventing pyroptosis and reducing the high levels of cytokines associated with severe cases of COVID-19. In the context of Euclidean space, a $k$-centers clustering is a fundamental structure that consists of the smallest set of $k$ balls with the lowest radius possible, covering the given point set. This paper focuses on the dynamic $k$-centers problem, where points are continuously added or removed from the set. Our primary concern is a one-sided update, either the inclusion of one point or the exclusion of one point. The ideal solution would provide the new optimal $k$-centers structure in $O(k)$ time. In this study, we show that in $d$-dimensional space, such an update can be achieved in $O(k \cdot k^d \log k)$ time. This result applies to a broad range of spaces, including $l_1$ and $l_\infty$ spaces, with slightly more complicated projections. This solution builds upon a recent approach by Cohen et al. and involves similar technical components, such as a randomized sampling technique and a local transformation method, both of which can be applied across different space metrics. These methods enable us to tackle additional problems, such as finding the largest $k$-centers structure or determining if a given set of points forms a $k$-centers structure. These problems can be solved in $O(k^{d+1} \log k)$ time. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach for the core problem and may provide insights for resolving other important questions in this domain. Additionally, we propose an approximation algorithm that can solve the basic $k$-centers problem in $O(\log k)$ time, with a radius accuracy of $O(\sqrt{k})$. This algorithm's performance is validated through extensive experiments, with notable results in data sets comprising up to $10^6$ points in $50$-dimensional space. These experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach over traditional methods, such as DBSCAN, for large data sets. As for static $k$-centers, our solution provides the first $O(k \cdot k^d \log k)$-approximation algorithm in $d$-dimensional space. This paper's algorithms have been implemented and are publicly available for download. It has further been applied in collaboration with a researcher at Google, yielding a positive outcome.  The source code for this project can be found at https://github.com/alexsandry/nearopt-kcenters. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. The model's code and data can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes. Finally, the proposed approach's superiority is validated by conducting a thorough ablation study, addressing potential drawbacks and model size-related issues. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent expanded convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked convolutional layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the model's reliability decreases with each subsequent layer due to decreasing dimensionality. To address this, QPNet is an autoregressive model comprising two types of layers: Pitch-dependent Expanded Convolution (PEC) layers and Bidirectional Expanded Convolution (BEC) layers. PEC layers are similar to WN layers but with input features based on the pitch estimate, and BEC layers are the reverse of WN layers with increased dimensionality, successfully generating quasi-periodic targets. By combining these layers, QPNet generates high-fidelity quasi-periodic raw waveforms with improved pitch control and overall performance. Experimental evaluations of speech and musical notes demonstrate QPNet's effectiveness against WN and a state-of-the-art generative model. Additionally, the model exhibits versatility in modeling various conditions, including pitch, spectrum, and noise. The proposed pitch-dependent expanded convolutional network shows promise as a versatile layer for generative raw waveform models. Planets within the habitable zones of their stars, having temperatures suitable for liquid water, don't necessarily guarantee the presence of life. To assess this, we recommend using spectroscopic techniques to analyze a planet's interaction with its star through stellar flux and the chemical composition of its atmosphere. This approach enables the identification of various biomarkers, such as oxygenated molecules, methane, and ozone, which can indicate different forms of life. By modeling the gas-filled Jovian exoplanets and combining our photochemical models with stellar flux and compositional data, we can determine the relative importance of absorption species in these planets' spectra. The outcome shows that gas-rich planets offer a more complex spectral pattern due to the abundant presence of water vapor, methane, and carbon dioxide. These planets exhibit a broader wavelength range than terrestrial worlds, extending from 0.4 micrometers to 0.1 millimeters. The detection of these biomarkers in gas-filled Jovian exoplanets is more challenging than in their smaller counterparts because the latter's greater surface gravity causes a more opaque atmosphere. Nevertheless, our models suggest that next-generation telescopes will be capable of identifying various forms of life on gas-filled Jovian exoplanets. Our research reveals that current noise localization methods in image analysis are ineffective due to poorly defined targets or easy image analysis, leading to unnecessary complications when there are overlapping shapes, diverse textures, and significant illumination variations. To overcome these challenges, we developed a theoretical framework to measure the ease of detecting visual noises and applied it to design an efficient noise detection algorithm. Our algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through comparative evaluations with state-of-the-art methods on diverse image datasets, showing consistent improvements in accuracy and computation speed. Furthermore, our approach is versatile, enabling seamless extension to other image analysis tasks such as segmentation, object detection, and style transfer. Additionally, a preliminary evaluation of our framework's potential to guide other image algorithms is presented, suggesting potential for future improvements and new features. In contrast to current methods, our algorithm achieves superior performance with less computational expense, but incurs a higher constant factor, resulting in inferior performance on simple images. Nonetheless, our results indicate that with more rigorous evaluation and optimization, our algorithm could rival the ease of other methods on straightforward images, while maintaining superior performance on more complex images. In such cases, the trade-off would be well worth the increased computational expense. The term 'challenging' refers to the level of difficulty associated with detecting a specific target in an image, incorporating not just the target's size and shape, but also all image characteristics that may affect detection, such as nearby shapes, diverse textures, and varying illumination. This perspective on image analysis is not unique to noise detection, and we expect it to also enhance the performance of other image analysis tasks, like segmentation, object detection, and style transfer, particularly on challenging images. This insight into the complexities of image analysis encourages the development of more robust algorithms that prioritize accuracy over speed and vice versa. In response to these considerations, we introduced the concept of highly accurate, slow noise detection algorithms and the term'state-of-the-art' methods that are fast but less accurate, hoping to engage other researchers in the ongoing debate about the trade-off between accuracy and computation time in image analysis. This discussion is not limited to noise detection

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves assessing whether a polyp is benign, adenomatous, or carcinomatous, and if adenomatous, evaluating its dysplastic content. This determination is usually made through the analysis of tissue samples following a step-wise approach by pathologists. Our research aims to streamline this process by developing an AI-powered system that automates polyp characterization and grading. To achieve this, we created the UniToPatho dataset consisting of histopathological images of colorectal polyps along with their characterization and grading information, collected from seven different institutions. This dataset comprises 9000 annotated regions of interest, resulting from the extraction of 3600 independent images, and is deemed the largest dataset of its kind to date. UniToPatho dataset is available for research use cases following strict data protection policies and protocols. In order to validate the consistency of the annotations within the dataset, a dedicated web-based platform was developed, enabling multiple pathologists to assess and compare the annotations in real-time, based on predefined characterization and grading guidelines. Language barriers pose significant challenges in global communication, and current translation techniques often struggle with switching between spoken and written text. Advanced neural models have made significant progress in translating written text across languages, but similar improvements have not been seen when it comes to spoken words. This lack of advancement means that people who can read but not hear a language may still face significant communication difficulties. For instance, a person who can understand written French but not spoken French may become confused listening to French audio, which includes subtitles they can read. Unfortunately, this person has no way to know what the spoken words are saying unless the subtitles match the text being spoken, which would not account for mistakes made by the translator. This problem highlights the need for voice-to-text translation capabilities that can translate spoken languages into written text, allowing people to easily understand voices in a foreign language. This technique would also enable text-to-speech synthesis based on the translated text, providing a full end-to-end translation service. Although this paper focuses on a specific trio of languages (English-to-French-to-English), it demonstrates the feasibility of the entire voice-to-text-and-speech-synthesis process and offers practical applications for consumers, such as translation software with no need for user input, as well as significant benefits for people with hearing impairments who rely on written subtitles to follow audio in a foreign language. This innovative approach to translation also paves the way for more complex combinations of written and spoken languages to be handled in a similar manner. Given that digital data does not need to be recompiled after each translation update, users can take full advantage of advanced neural model improvements with zero effort, making this technology even more useful over time. This paper introduces a zero-shot voice translation model based on neural multilingual learning techniques, which allows it to translate unseen speech-to-text pairs given it has learned from numerous related written text translations. This model leverages massive datasets of cross-language text by using a system that can convert spoken language into written text and vice versa, ensuring that it can learn from a vast amount of data simultaneously. Although this model shows near-state-of-the-art performance when comparing spoken and written versions of the same language, performance drops when translating spoken French into written English, likely due to the larger vocabulary differences between these two languages. This model achieves this level of translation capability with just two giant datasets, essentially achieving state-of-the-art results with just one dataset for similar speech-to-speech translation tasks.
